Target 11 In Sri Lanka, several large-scale restoration projects utilize Nature-based Solutions (NbS) and Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EbA) to enhance climate resilience, ranging from mountain watersheds to coastal lagoons. 1. Forest & Watershed Restoration (Drought & Water Security) These projects focus on restoring degraded catchments to regulate water flow, stabilize slopes, and ensure community access to water during dry seasons. Climate Resilient Integrated Water Management Project (CRIWMP) : A major initiative funded by the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and implemented by UNDP Sri Lanka. It focuses on the Mi Oya, Malwathu Oya, and Yan Oya river basins. By reforesting watersheds and desilting ancient "cascade" tank systems, the project has improved water security for over 1.2 million people , ensuring irrigation and drinking water even during severe droughts. Project CORE (Climate-smart Opportunities through Restoration and Education) : A collaboration between IUCN Sri Lanka , the Forest Department, and HSBC. In June 2025, it successfully restored degraded lands in Thanthirimale using 19 native tree species to rebuild forest resilience and stabilize local ecosystems. Emerald Trails Initiative : Led by WNPS PLANT and Alliance Finance at Radella Estate , this project is establishing a 13 km forest corridor. It aims to restore biodiversity, stabilize watersheds, and provide long-term livelihoods in the central highlands. "Clean Sri Lanka" 1,000-Acre Project : Launched in April 2025 , this public-private partnership aims to plant 1,000 acres of forest to safeguard biodiversity and enhance national forest cover. 2. Mangrove Restoration (Storm & Coastal Protection) Sri Lanka’s mangrove restoration was recognized as a UN World Restoration Flagship in 2024 for its science-based and community-led success. National Mangrove Conservation Project : Supported by Seacology , this project helps coastal communities (especially women-led groups) protect and replant mangroves. These forests act as critical bio-shields against storm surges, cyclones, and coastal erosion. Blue-Green Protectors : A joint project by SLYCAN Trust and MEPA targeting the North and South provinces. Notable sites include Jaffna, Mannar, and Puttalam, where restoration efforts enhance coastal livelihoods and provide natural protection for vulnerable fishing villages. Vidattaltivu Restoration : Following a 2024 legal challenge, the government committed in August 2025 to restore protection for the ecologically vital Vidattaltivu mangrove patch, a key site for regional storm protection. Mannar Landscape Project : A UNDP/GEF SGP initiative that combines mangrove planting with soil and water conservation and waste management to build climate-resilient coastal communities. 3. Tourism related projects: Restoration and Urban Development : The Metro Colombo Urban Development Project has successfully restored many abandoned and polluted sites, transforming them into a network of parks, recreational zones, walking tracks, and event spaces. These initiatives have significantly enhanced urban biodiversity while delivering substantial economic benefits to Colombo and its suburbs. Community Opportunities in Tourism : Continued tourism development has generated diverse opportunities for local communities, particularly in the wildlife , coastal , and hill country destinations. As these regions grow in popularity among international and domestic travelers, their overall contribution to the national economy continues to rise. Economic Impact of Conservation : A key indicator of tourism’s sectoral success is the annual revenue generated through ticket sales at National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, and Forest Reserves, which directly supports conservation funding and local livelihoods.
Key Challenges Summary: Target 2 The Key Challenges  of Target 1 also apply here. Those that ar e specific to this target are: The most important being the reluctance of government agencies (with the exception of the DWC) in sharing spatial information data on protected areas, restored areas  and other forms of biodiversity interventions. The wide distribution of data into many government organisations with the absence of a central data gathering, tracking and evaluation The very wide continuum of actions that come under the term restoration requires greater analysis for what is most relevant and feasible for Sri Lanka. A ‘classification or taxonomy’ of restoration activities practised is required. In particular traditional methods of restoration used by some local communities need to include into mainstream actions Introduction of new technologies and scientific tools for restoration. While the Sri Lanka scientific community does apply some of these, they need to apply by the wider community of practitioners who lie outside academia At present only a very few projects can be considered as conducting ecological restoration (in its scientific sense) while many others that also contribute to restoration of degraded areas Despite very commendable efforts, the non-availability of scientifically valid and reliable data from the private sector restoration projects with the exception of a few. With brief descriptions of their project activities The invisibility of the actions and data collected by sectoral and regional organisations, civil society organisations etc. as they are not represented in nationally accepted data bases and nor are these types of data easily accessible Absence of quality control of data on major biodiversity related actions of state sector organisations that result in a wide range of approaches that does not allow data aggregation or reliable analyses Target 11 Key Challenges: Limited public and development agency recognition of the importance of ecosystem goods and services, Absence of PES and related instruments that formally recognise nature's contributions to people; absence of integration into national accounting systems, Low levels of consideration in sectoral plans and programmes Much of the work is fragmented It is difficult to identify actual progress in development of instruments and its current status of inclusion into strategies and actions of national and sectoral strategies and actions No proper waste management system, treatment facilities of industrial and hazardous waste, For medical waste, for example Approaches for Further Implementation: National Registry and Valuation: Establish and validate a nationally recognized register of Nature’s Contributions to People (NCP) to standardize data collection. This includes developing a robust valuation framework to quantify the economic and social worth of ecosystem goods and services. Indigenous and Local Knowledge: Formally recognize and protect the contributions of NCPs as practiced and preserved by indigenous communities, ensuring their traditional ecological knowledge is integrated into modern conservation. Economic Integration: Incorporate NCP values into National Accounting Systems and Gross Domestic Product (GDP) calculations to reflect the true environmental cost and benefit of national development. Institutional Mainstreaming: Foster deep awareness of NCPs within government development agencies and mandate their integration into Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) frameworks. Corporate and Private Sector Engagement: Drive a shift in business attitudes by encouraging Natural Capital Accounting and emphasizing the long-term dependency of commercial industries on stable ecosystem services. Public Advocacy and Literacy: Launch targeted campaigns to improve public recognition of NCPs, moving beyond general environmentalism to a specific understanding of how nature supports daily livelihoods, health, and disaster resilience.

It’s key features are: Restoring Ecosystem Functions : Hydrological Regulation : It resuscitates ancient "Cascade Tank Systems" —interconnected series of small reservoirs that act as a nature-based solution to regulate water flow. This system captures excess rainwater to prevent floods and releases it slowly to maintain water availability during dry seasons. Disease Risk Reduction : Restoring these systems provides safer, filtered groundwater, which is critical in areas where poor water quality is linked to Chronic Kidney Disease (CKDu) . Recent examples such as the urban wetland management plan of Gothatuwa Wetland Park (2025-2029) (Source) Currently the SLLDC manages four marshes: Kotte Marsh – 233.6 acres Kolonnawa wetland - 380 Acres Heen Ela Marsh - 206.154 Acres Parliament Upper Retention Area – 69.6 acres Figure 5 : Urban Wet land Map TARGET 1_Figure 5.pdf Urban Wetlands, Biodiversity, Recreation and Climate change Dr. W.D.C.T Gunasiri, chethikagunasiri@gmail.com , Environmental Scientist, Sri Lanka Land Development Corporation, Welikada, Sri Lanka An Overview of the SLLDC Wetland Biodiversity Conservation Programmes The Colombo District Low-Lying Areas Development Board was established in 1968 under Act No. 15 of 1968 (COLOMBO DISTRICT (LOW-LYING AREAS) RECLAMATION AND BOARD ACT, NO.15 OF 1968, 1968). Its mandate was to reclaim and develop marshy and low-lying areas and to retain custody, management, and control of vested lands. The institution was subsequently re-designated as the Sri Lanka Land Development Corporation (SLLDC) through legislative amendments, including Act No. 52 of 1982 and Act No. 13 of 2021 (COLOMBO DISTRICT (LOW-LYING AREAS) RECLAMATION AND DEVELOPMENT BOARD (AMENDMENT) ACT, No 52 of 1982, 1982; SRI LANKA LAND DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION (AMENDMENT) ACT, No. 13 OF 2021, 2021). Under a Cabinet decision dated 15 August 1996 (No. 96/1760/111/125), 390 hectares of low-lying lands surrounding the Parliament Lake were vested with SLLDC for flood protection purposes. These areas include the Kolonnawa, Kotte, and Heen Ela wetlands, as well as the Parliament Upper Retention Areas. See Figure 3 : Urban Wetland Map The Colombo Wetland Complex (CWC) is located within the Colombo hydrological boundary. It comprises a mosaic of interconnected wetlands linked through the Colombo canal network, and wetlands managed by SLLDC constitute a significant component of the complex. Under the World Bank-funded Metro Colombo Urban Development Project, the Wetland Management Strategy for the Colombo Metropolitan Region was developed in 2016 (Signes, 2016a). The strategy was based on comprehensive social, ecological, and economic assessments. It identified the CWC as covering approximately 1,900 hectares and comprising seven distinct habitat types (Signes, 2016b). Further, according to the Ecological Status Report of the Colombo Wetland Management Strategy,  275 animal species and 285 plant species were recorded within the CWC (Signes, 2016b). These include endemic and threatened species, as well as approximately 25 migratory bird species (Signes, 2016b). In addition, SLLDC established a dedicated Wetland Management Division in 2013 to strengthen urban wetland governance based on the principle of wise use. The Division also provides technical guidance for urban wetland restoration and management across the country. At present, SLLDC manages urban wetlands, particularly in Colombo, primarily as flood retention areas. At the same time, it enhances multiple ecosystem services. These include biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, and urban well-being. SLLDC also led the national process that resulted in Colombo receiving Ramsar Wetland City Accreditation in 2018, recognizing the international importance of the Colombo Wetland Complex. At present, SLLDC manages urban wetlands, particularly in Colombo primarily as flood retention areas while enhancing multiple ecosystem services, including biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, and urban well-being, through wetland restoration, wetland park development, invasive species management, strategic planning, and public awareness programmes (Signes, 2016a). Programmes and projects Wetland Encroachment Prevention at Gothatuwa Wetland (2020–2024) This programme focuses on preventing illegal encroachment and restoring degraded areas of the Gothatuwa Wetland, while safeguarding its flood retention function and improving habitat conditions for wetland biodiversity. Development of Gothatuwa Wetland Park (ongoing) The Gothatuwa Wetland Park project aims to restore wetland ecosystems and enhance biodiversity while developing the site as a public wetland park for environmental education, awareness, and community engagement. Floating Wetlands for Urban Water Quality Improvement (2021- up to date) SLLDC has introduced floating wetlands as nature-based solutions for water purification in Beira Lake and other urban waterways in Colombo. These interventions improve water quality, attract bird species, and enhance the aesthetic value of degraded water bodies. Urban Wetlands for Flood Mitigation and Land-Use Regulation (on going) SLLDC manages urban wetlands as nature-based solutions for flood control and regulates low-lying land filling and development through hydrological assessments and drainage approvals. Flood mitigation projects in high-risk areas integrate engineered structures with wetland restoration. Carbon Sequestration Assessment of the Colombo Wetland Complex (on going) SLLDC is undertaking an assessment of the carbon sequestration capacity of the Colombo Wetland Complex to strengthen the evidence base for integrating urban wetlands into national climate change mitigation efforts Canal Network Maintenance and Invasive Species Management (on going) SLLDC conducts regular maintenance of the Colombo Canal Network, including the removal of aquatic invasive species that obstruct water flow. The Corporation also regulates treated wastewater discharges into the Colombo Canal System. Institutional Coordination and Community Engagement (on going) SLLDC actively coordinates with relevant government agencies through mechanisms such as the National Wetland Steering Committee and provides technical expertise in hydrology and urban wetland management. Community engagement is facilitated through wetland parks such as Diyasaru Park and Gothatuwa Wetland Park, with local communities involved in biodiversity monitoring, invasive species removal, and awareness programmes. The Future With increasing climate change impacts, the role of the Sri Lanka Land Development Corporation (SLLDC) in urban flood mitigation and in maintaining pollution-free urban water bodies will become increasingly essential and critical. To address these emerging challenges, SLLDC will utilize wetlands under its jurisdiction as nature-based solutions for climate adaptation and mitigation. These wetlands will be managed primarily for flood mitigation while enhancing multiple ecosystem services, including water purification, climate regulation, and wetland-based tourism and recreation, in accordance with the principle of wise use of wetlands. Moreover, the institution will also provide its technical expertise for urban wetland restoration and management islandwide. Central Highlands of Sri Lanka - In this report, the evidence from actions for targets 1 to 4 and some others across many state organizations, the academia conducting research, the private sector and participatory local communities,  developing and  implementing spatial plans associated with  biodiversity conservation consistently reinforces the high conservation values in  outside- of- protected -areas locations.  The critical role of Sri Lanka’s Central Highlands is one of the best examples to illustrate this phenomenon.  This is due to its high biodiversity, endemism; presence of critical habitats for many species;  the presence of sub river basins that harbor Evolutionary Significant Units (ESUs) 1 (see the section on In Situ Conservation of Freshwater fish in Target 4); water resource sustenance as the origin of the major rivers;   the identification of it as a ‘fragile’ area by  national physical plans beyond 2030;  repeatedly  identified as a target region  of many external donor funded projects (see project list under the BD of the MoE in Section I and  the LDN Target Setting project above )  among other evidence cited in this report. Most  importantly, the serious environmental and human  impacts in the Central Highlands Region caused by November 2025 Cyclone Ditwah speaks louder than any words of its critical relevance for biodiversity, the impacts of climate change and the socio economic framework of the entire country. Progress Summary: Summary of progress - All major government stakeholders of biodiversity conservation (DWC, FD) have adopted biodiversity inclusive spatial planning with varying degrees of participation. They are being implemented with varying levels of success. The CEA, CC& CRMD and the DFAR  combine application of  biodiversity inclusive planning partially as they have to reconcile development activities with biodiversity values. The DFAR that deals with fisheries and aquatic resources through its FMAs implements biodiversity inclusive participatory management. The LUPPD spatial plans are integrated, participatory and biodiversity inclusive at GN level (smallest administrative unit) and the one above it the Divisional Secretariat. Current work is ongoing to develop district and then provincial level plans by the LUPPD. The National Physical Planning Department, Urban Development Authority and the SLLDC also play significant roles in national scale and urban area planning . Sri Lanka Navy has spatial data on coral reefs while the National Aquatic Resources Research and Development Agency develops hydrographic maps. See Annex 1.1- Marine Spatial Map of Weligama Area Annex 1.1.pdf Thus, sectoral datasets on land use, coastal and marine use and areas outside of PAs of conservation importance (potential OECMs) are available. A number of projects on identification of land, coastal and marine areas that can contribute to a nationally applicable category of OECMs are currently underway. These are expected to  fine tune existing information on potential OECMs to achieve national and global biodiversity targets of the KMGBF. Ongoing efforts at sectoral levels to integrate biodiversity into all actions of planning through donor funded projects, training of key government stakeholder organizations through technology transfer and application of modern spatial planning tools provide hope that all main components of Target 1 will be implemented
Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges Policy Gap : The absence of implementation of a National Land Use Policy that is biodiversity inclusive, addresses land, coastal and marine use to reduce the loss of high biodiversity areas and is participatory including the rights of indigenous communities. This leads to distributed mandates and  sometimes conflicting mandates of key stakeholders Institutional inadequacy, Fragmentation:: Currently sectoral spatial plans with the attributes important for biodiversity conservation  are carried out by a large number of government agencies which is fragmented, leading to often un-coordinated and conflicting results. Poor cooperation within and between institutions; inadequate funding; weak enforcement; development and implementation of sectoral and sub national projects and actions  without meaningful collaboration and consultation are factors. Institutional memory - The sharp discontinuity of work during transition periods by officer transfers/ replacement or retirement in government organizations is wasteful of time, effort and resources by all stakeholders. Non-implementation - The spatial plans already developed by government agencies are weakly enforced with an absence of an adequate monitoring system. Lack of reliable medium to longer term impact evaluation and or effectiveness of biodiversity inclusive spatial planning- While there are many end- of- programme or activity evaluation reports, they are often very short term and do not provide reliable and verifiable evidence of impacts. Most agencies that carry out spatial plans apply management measures. However, their effectiveness cannot be established due to absence of data that links it to management tools Data : Absence of centralized data gathering, compiling and monitoring system for state institutions. Coupled with the high degree of resistance to sharing official data, this is a huge, fundamental and a cross-cutting flaw that negatively affects progress on the entire KMGBF as well as on all environment related actions. This is a significant factor causing long delays in implementation and evaluation of results of all actions and waste of time, effort and resources. Inadequate staff capacity is a major factor that hinders  ground truthing, field surveys on land and coastal areas  Verifications are essential for reliable boundary demarcation of spatial plans. Socio Economic Challenges: Multi-dimensional p overty levels especially in rural areas with low economic opportunities works against mainstream biodiversity conservation actions. This situation appears to have been exacerbated since the Covid 19 epidemic and its subsequent impacts on whole of society Public Acceptance: The attitudinal change (a form of transformational change) required by a large proportion of Sri Lankan society towards effective implementation of local level biodiversity inclusive plans is a key challenge Time periods for significant impacts : Impacts of programmes and activities on biodiversity conservation are realised over a longer time period and need to be monitored over such periods continuously and consistently. Longer term impact evaluation is nearly absent. This leads to loss of recorded results, waste of funding and is a setback to progress along sustainable development pathways. Different Approaches for further implementation Addressing institutional inadequacies including fragmentation; reducing overlap of mandates of government stakeholders; implementing actual cooperation between organisations; implementing modern management systems in government organisations that carry out spatial planning. The Ocean Country Partnership Project (OCPP) supported by the United Kingdom (government, NGO and academia partners) implemented spatial plans for coastal habitats  of Sri Lanka. This work is not yet complete. Providing access to improved modeling and risk assessment tools that combine climate change threats. However, ‘last mile’ information is vital for robust spatial plans that are reliable and verifiable to a high degree of accuracy. A central data system that acts as a hub linked to all organisations conducting biodiversity related work and can provide data on scientific, technical, socio economic and state of progress on the KMGBF, the SDGs and related agreements and conventions is vital

Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges Absence of a national land use policy. This has been referred to in Target 1. Encroachment, poaching and invasives: The constant battle of protected area authorities with illegal encroachers, poachers and deforestation by marginal communities continues. Spread of invasive species also an emerging threat. Development pressures -Expanding populations driven by the need for agricultural land, settlements fueled by economic development, drive loss and fragmentation of natural habitats exert continuous pressure on protected areas despite commendable efforts by protected area authorities. Conflicting policy decisions also contribute. Inadequate resources for enhanced protection - Human resources remain highly inadequate. Field level protection requires working under difficult field conditions with less rewards than working in a city office. The use of advanced technology may help to alleviate this problem, but still the need for vigilance on the ground remains. Funding constraints are another challenge Low number of scientific studies on population sizes within protected areas , spatial and temporal population trends; genetic diversity;  habitat occupancy and major life history attributes hamper better conservation efforts. The exception to this is the Sri Lanka wild elephants and few other research. Different approaches While Sri Lanka does not have a legally recognized OECM classification at present actions are being taken to establish OECMs  (See Target 1) . These are likely to yield the  benefits for extended protection after implementation. Action Effectiveness Summary: CASE 1- Ex situ Case one to body Ex-situ conservation in Sri Lanka CASE- 1.docx Ex-situ conservation in Sri Lanka Hiranya Sudasinghe* and Rohan Pethiyagoda** *      Division of Evolutionary Ecology, Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland; and Naturhistorisches Museum Bern, Bern, Switzerland, hsudasinghe@gmail.com **   Wildlife Heritage Trust, 117 Park Road, Colombo 5; and Ichthyology Division, Australian Museum, Sydney, Australia, rohanpet@gmail.com Introduction – The overwhelming majority of the hundreds of species of Sri Lankan plants and animals assessed as Critically Endangered (CR) have been so assessed because they are narrow-range endemics with areas of occupancy less than 10 sq. km. As a result, they are vulnerable to local threats such as land-use change, pollution, landslides, extreme weather, and fire. The stochastic nature of these threats mandates that ex-situ conservation measures be adopted, so that reserve populations are available in the event of the wild population being extirpated. Sri Lanka’s CR species need to be considered, however, in the light of a suite of unusual factors, briefly outlined as follows: Taxonomic Uncertainty and Sampling bias - Because the taxonomy is out of date, species that should correctly be assessed as Data Deficient (DD) are often placed in the CR category. In the case of the 12 species of CR freshwater fishes, for example, recent taxonomic work has shown three to be synonyms, three to have ranges greatly exceeding 10 sq. km., and two to be DD. Thus, only four CR species are deserving of immediate conservation attention. Freshwater crabs - The distributions of 34 species of CR freshwater crabs too, are known from only a single survey project that was focused on taxonomy rather than population / range estimation (Bahir et al., 2005a). As a result, many species that may enjoy wider distributions may be, because of a deficiency in sampling, categorized as narrow-range and hence CR. Because the reliable identification of these crabs calls for the euthanization and dissection of specimens to establish their identity, their CR status (and consequent listing as Strictly Protected in the conservation legislation) means that permission to conduct reliable surveys is difficult to obtain. As a result, no surveys have been conducted over the past two decades, widening the knowledge gap still further. Hog Deer- Another example is the Hog Deer, Axis porcinus, which is known from a population spanning the cinnamon-growing region between the Bentara and Gin rivers of south-western Sri Lanka. The species was assessed as CR in 2012 and strictly protected. The natural range of A. porcinus, however, is in the sub-Himalayan region between the Indus and Irrawaddy rivers. Given that feral populations of these species are known from Hawaii, Florida, South Africa, the Indian Peninsula, and southern Australia, it seems almost certain that the Sri Lankan population too, is feral. It probably stems from individuals that were carried as live food on a sailing vessel from Kolkata and released in the port of Galle some time prior to 1860. There is strong evidence that this founder population had already hybridized with chital deer (Axis axis) prior to release in Sri Lanka (Hill et al., 2019). It appears therefore that this species is worthy neither of its CR status nor further conservation attention. It is important, therefore, that surveys and taxonomic research be promoted to re-evaluate the taxonomic and conservation status of every CR species. The value of such surveys is underlined by an ongoing national survey of the angiosperm flora by the National Institute for Fundamental Studies (NIFS) instituted in 2015. The 2012 National Red List assesses five species as Extinct (EX), two as Extinct in the Wild (EW), and 177 as CR (Possibly Extinct) (CR-PE). To date, the NIFS survey has rediscovered three of the five EX species, both EW species and more than 100 of the CR-PE species. What is more, the survey also discovered some 150 new species new to science (Jayasinghe, 2025). Ex-situ Conservation While the Departments of National Zoological Gardens (DNZG) and National Botanic Gardens (DNBG) would be the natural foci for the ex-situ conservation of animals and plants in Sri Lanka, neither has been awarded a national mandate to undertake this activity. Nevertheless, both institutions have shown interest in maintaining ex-situ populations, even if not on a systematic basis. Freshwater fish- The Zoo, for example, maintains a population of Pethia bandula and Systomus asoka, both CR. It has successfully bred the former, establishing a captive population of almost 1000 individuals. Meanwhile, the single stream in which the wild population occurs has been declared a sanctuary by the Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC), which has also undertaken awareness-building initiatives with the local communities associated with both species. Systomus asoka, however, is a recalcitrant species: attempts to breed it over several decades have proved futile. Plants - Meanwhile, the Wildlife and Nature Protection Society (WNPS), the country’s largest and oldest environmental NGO, has initiated an ex-situ conservation project for 52 species of CR plants utilizing a five-year funding window made available by Hemas, a large Sri Lankan corporate. Importantly, WNPS has the capacity to substantially expand this project in the future. The role of cryopreservation and seed banks for wild plants remains to be established in Sri Lanka, however. The Plant Genetic Resources Centre in Gannoruwa has substantial capacity with regard to crop species and provides opportunities for applying its technology and expertise to wild plants as well. Amphibians - With 17 species formally declared EX, Sri Lanka’s highly endemic amphibian fauna is considered to be particularly at risk. Ten of the 15 CR species belong to the shrub-frog genus Pseudophilautus, which benefited from an early ex-situ conservation initiative by the Wildlife Heritage Trust (Bahir et al., 2005b). As a result, the reproductive biology of these frogs is well understood, and they are likely to be relatively easy to breed and maintain in captivity. Of the remaining five species of CR amphibians, however (Taruga fastigo, Duttaphrynus noellerti, Microhyla karunaratnei, Adenomus kandianus and Lankanectes pera), attempts at captive breeding have been made, so far abortively, only with regard to the last (R. Pethiyagoda, pers. comm.). Among the others, A. kandianus too, can be expected to be challenging given that it breeds in fast-flowing mountain streams. Future Directions Though thus far informal, discussions have taken place with a view to formally mandating DNZG and DNBG to initiate ex-situ programmes for CR species, with responsibility also to monitor the relevant wild populations, ensuring their survival. At the same time, DWC recognizes the importance of in-situ conservation, regarding ex-situ as an option of last resort. As evidenced by the WNPS-Hemas project and several other public- private partnerships though not as extensive or in depth as the former, DWC already recognizes the contribution that non-government initiatives could make with regard to ex-situ programmes. Future public-private ex-situ partnerships with clear conservation objectives if implemented as they should be, are likely to make an increasing contribution in the near term. CASE- 2 Distribution of Endemic Flowering Plants in Sri Lanka and the Impacts of Cyclonic Storm Ditwah CASE- 2.docx Distribution of Endemic Flowering Plants in Sri Lanka and the Impacts of Cyclonic Storm Ditwah Professor Siril Wijesundara, National Institute of Fundamental Studies, Kandy, Sri Lanka 1. Introduction Recent Cyclonic Storm Ditwah have emphasized the growing threat posed by climate-related disasters to biodiversity in Sri Lanka. Understanding the spatial distribution of endemic species and their exposure to cyclone impact is therefore essential for effective conservation and disaster management. 2. Endemic Flowering Plants of Sri Lanka Endemism refers to the ecological condition in which a species is confined to a defined geographical area and has originated there. Sri Lanka supports 3,087 indigenous angiosperm species belonging to 186 plant families, of which 863 species are endemic. These endemic flowering plants represent a wide range of life forms, including trees, shrubs, herbs, climbers, and epiphytes. Many of these species exhibit narrow ecological tolerances and are restricted to specific climatic and altitudinal zones. Globally, endemic species tend to be concentrated in biodiversity hotspots, and Sri Lanka exhibits a moderate to high level of endemism relative to its size. The distribution of endemic flowering plants across the island is not random; instead, it follows distinct geographical and climatic patterns shaped by rainfall, elevation, and historical forest stability. 3. Spatial Distribution and Endemic Areas In a study conducted by us in 2016, the spatial distribution of endemic flowering plants in Sri Lanka has been analyzed using species occurrence records from the National Herbarium and reliable ecological studies. These data were plotted using Geographic Information System (GIS) techniques. Sri Lanka was divided into 2,847 grid cells, each measuring 5 km × 5 km, and a total of 84,429 location records were analyzed. Weighted endemism values were calculated for each grid cell to identify regions with high concentrations of endemic species. Based on this analysis, nine major endemic areas were identified where weighted endemism values ranged between 0.7 and 2.5. These areas are the Central Highlands, South Western Wet Zone, Northern Highlands, Eastern Highlands, Ritigala, Dolu Kanda, Yala, Wilpattu, and Jaffna. Among these, the wet zone and central highlands exhibit the highest levels of endemism, emphasizing the importance of high rainfall and stable climatic conditions in maintaining endemic plant diversity. Within these nine endemic areas, several core endemic areas were recognized due to exceptionally high species richness and uniqueness. These include Sinharaja, Adam’s Peak, Knuckles, Horton Plains, and Kandy. These core zones support not only large numbers of endemic species but also endemic genera such as Doona, Stemonoporus, Hortonia, Schumacheria, and Loxococcus, many of which are largely confined to wet-zone forests. The restricted distribution of these genera further highlights the conservation importance of these regions. 4. Cyclonic Storm Ditwah and Its Impacts Cyclonic Storm Ditwah, which developed in the Bay of Bengal, significantly influenced weather conditions in Sri Lanka through intense rainfall, strong winds, and widespread flooding. In addition to causing severe landslides, its rain bands caused major hydrological disturbances across the island, particularly affecting the wet zone, central highlands, and parts of the intermediate zone. These regions overlap strongly with Sri Lanka’s principal endemic and core endemic plant areas. In the Central Highlands, prolonged heavy rainfall associated with Ditwah triggered landslides, soil erosion, and slope instability, especially in montane forests such as Knuckles, Horton Plains, and Adam’s Peak. Many endemic flowering plants in these areas occupy narrow altitudinal belts and specialized microhabitats. Landslides can completely remove vegetation cover, leading to the local extinction of endemic species with limited distribution ranges. In the Southwestern Wet Zone, including areas surrounding Sinharaja, intense rainfall led to flooding and prolonged soil saturation. These conditions negatively affect endemic herbs, shrubs, and understory plants by reducing soil oxygen levels and increasing susceptibility to disease. Strong winds also caused canopy damage, altering forest structure and microclimatic conditions that are essential for the regeneration of endemic tree species. An additional indirect impact of Cyclonic Storm Ditwah is the increased vulnerability of disturbed habitats to invasive alien plant species. Landslide scars, flood-damaged forests, and windthrown gaps provide ideal conditions for invasive species to establish and spread, posing long-term threats to endemic flowering plants through competition and habitat alteration. 5. Importance of GIS-Based Overlay Analysis Overlaying endemic flowering plant distribution maps with GIS-based cyclone impact data, such as rainfall intensity, flood extent, and landslide susceptibility, is an extremely useful approach for conservation and disaster risk management. Such spatial overlays allow identification of areas where high endemic richness coincides with high disaster exposure. For example, overlaying endemic plant hotspots with Cyclonic Storm Ditwah impact zones can help: Identify endemic-rich areas that experienced the greatest disturbance, Prioritize sites for post-cyclone ecological monitoring and restoration, Guide land-use planning to minimize development in sensitive endemic zones, and Support climate change adaptation strategies aimed at reducing biodiversity loss. GIS-based analyses also enable scenario modeling to assess how future cyclones may affect endemic plant distributions, providing valuable information for long-term conservation planning. Sri Lanka’s endemic flowering plants are a globally significant and irreplaceable component of biodiversity, with their distribution strongly concentrated in the wet zone and central highlands. Cyclonic Storm Ditwah demonstrated how extreme weather events can pose serious threats to these endemic-rich regions through flooding, landslides, and habitat disturbance. The strong spatial overlap between endemic plant hotspots and cyclone-affected areas emphasizes the need for integrated approaches that combine biodiversity data with disaster risk assessments. Overlaying endemic plant distributions on GIS maps of cyclone impacts is a powerful and practical tool for identifying vulnerable areas, guiding conservation priorities, and enhancing the resilience of Sri Lanka’s unique floral diversity in the face of increasing climatic extremes.

Progress Summary: A key policy framework exists A number of regulations have been in place since several decades ago prior to the explicit recognition of IAS as a major threat to biodiversity in the Convention on Biological Diversity. The importance of IAS as a serious threat to agriculture, a major livelihood of Sri Lankans, is well recognised through a range of programmes and actions instituted by the Department of Agriculture. Inland freshwater fisheries particularly in tanks (man-made reservoirs) that are sites of community based inland fisheries and important sources of protein for the local communities is another serious threat by IAS. Actions are being taken by the National Aquatic Research and Development Agency (NARA). See below. An increasing number of scientific research publications on IAS species, their impacts and factors driving introductions and establishment among others is available. These highlight the threats to livelihoods often of rural agriculture-based communities and the vital need for adequate enforcement of existing regulations and the need to embrace new tools and strategies to prevent introductions, establishment and spread of IAS
Key Challenges Summary: Key challenges Policy Gap : There is no policy on Biosecurity. Such a policy has become very relevant given the prominent threats posed by IAS and the current interaction of IAS with climate change as well as other drivers of biodiversity loss (source). Regulatory Gap - While there is a national policy on IAS ( The National Policy on Invasive Alien Species (IAS) in Sri Lanka, Strategies and Action Plan ) there is no enacted legal instrument specifically on IAS.  Thus, although there are lists of invasive flora and fauna with well-known negative impacts they cannot be applied in enforcement unless through a legal instrument of a sectoral agency.  However, act on IAS is initiated to be developed. At present, Sri Lanka Customs can prevent the entry of suspected consignments at port of entries but they only destroy, or release based on the technical advice from other government agencies. Distributed institutions and mandates - There are a number of sectoral agencies and divisions within government ministries that are mandated to address IAS introductions, spread and establishment. The distributed system of responsibility does not have a formal mechanism for continuous collection and validation of data on IAS entry , establishment and spread . This absence contributes to the inability to track all phases of IAS in Sri Lanka and leads to unintentional as well as deliberate introductions. (source our article?) Weak enforcement - The horticultural trade and the ornamental fish and invertebrate trade are generally accepted to be the two most important commercial activities that have and appear to be currently contributing to introduction and spread of IAS. As these are both viewed primarily from a commercial and livelihood perspective there is no enforcement action even if there is violation of the National Plant Protection act?? Inadequate Capacity and Training : Low technical capacity in identification of potential IAS at entry, assessing impacts on biodiversity, modelling interactions between IAS and climate change, land and sea use change  etc. Insufficient scientific knowledge on established IAS - Except on Salvinia molesta and Eichornia crassipes , and impacts of invasive fish on inland fisheries. Sri Lanka lacks in depth knowledge of the impacts of established IAS. Except for the NPQS, organisations in charge of ports of entry and exit lack sufficient advanced tools and training for IAS identification and prevention of entry. Newer and advanced tools - There is a wide range of modelling, risk assessment and ‘horizon scanning’ methods applied for reducing potential IAS and management of introduced and established IAS. (IPBES 2023).  Many of these are not applied in Sri Lanka even though the scientific expertise to do so exist within the country. Public attitudes: Except in the case of agricultural weeds and invasive fish in tanks with community level inland fishery industry, the public is unaware of the importance of IAS including already established IAS plants and animals. The tendency of Sri Lankans  to include colorful and attractive foreign plants as part of home gardens provides a ready demand for invasive plants brought illegally into Sri Lanka. Public opposition to destroying animals even though they may be pests and invasives is a dimension that needs attention. Many control and eradication methods that are used in other countries are not acceptable. Different approaches to be taken for further implementation The Prevention and Control of Invasive Alien Species (IAS) for Enhanced Biosecurity Project soon to be implemented in Sri Lanka  ( 2026 -2027) will be commencing soon. It is expected to close the most important need for a biosecurity approach to IAS. The project covering both fauna and flora aims to trigger transformational change in Sri Lanka by addressing the root causes of biodiversity loss linked to IAS. It is national in scope and will include an initial national implementation. Land and Freshwater systems come under its scope. The main objective is to establish a comprehensive, institutionalized biosecurity framework that prevents future invasions, mitigate current impacts, and build long-term ecosystem resilience. Further, the project aims to update the policy, legal, operational and institutional framework for effective IAS control. This will accelerate and upscale implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) by delivering systemic, scalable solutions to one of the country’s most critical biodiversity threats. There are two main outcomes:  Institutionalized comprehensive IAS prevention measures in Sri Lanka and Reduced IAS pressure and livelihoods improved through sustained, partnership driven IAS management. Progress of work initiated by the Biodiversity Division on IAS- Update of the fauna IAS list and finalization of the updated flora list will take place in 2026. This will enable application of this list to the project to be launched soon. Use of research on IAS carried out by researchers- There is considerable body of research that is available on IAS flora and to a lesser degree on fauna. This research ought to be better integrated into sectoral and national decision making on all phases of IAS (forecasting, introduction, establishment and spread). Newer digital tools and mathematical models applied for better decision making and forecasting should be applied in Sri Lanka. A comprehensive global assessment of the IAS is available in the Thematic Assessment Report of Invasive Alien Species and their Control (IPBES 2023) ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7430692 )

Improved Market Compliance: over 1,300 quality tests conducted; 136+ sales outlets inspections performed, in 2024. The project aims to strengthen institutional capacity to promote safe, high-quality crop production, reducing the health and environmental risks of agrochemical misuse while improving export compliance. Implementation activities focus on promoting Good Agricultural Practices (GAP), conducting farmer training and workshops, and developing Comprehensive Action Plans for pesticide and fertilizer management. The initiative targets key agricultural districts including Nuwara Eliya, Matale, Anuradhapura, Puttalam, and Badulla, supporting safer and more sustainable crop production in line with biodiversity-friendly agricultural practices. https://safe.doa.gov.lk/?utm_source=chatgpt.com Field Survey on Incidences Monitoring and Occupational Exposure Study of Highly Hazardous Pesticide (HHPs) and Severely Hazardous Pesticide Formulations (SHPF) Among Farmers in Sri Lanka (2019-2020). The project was developed by the Designated National Authority, Office of the Registrar of Pesticides, Department of Agriculture of Sri Lanka, in collaboration with the Rotterdam Convention Secretariat and FAO representation in Sri Lanka. Main Actions Summary: As the overarching threat not only to biodiversity but to all life on this planet, climate change has risen rapidly in the national discourse over the past decade, The importance of climate change is reinforced by the extreme weather events experienced by Sri Lanka  (most recent example being November 2025 Cyclone Ditwah) that brings large scale destruction through severe flooding, earth slips and land slides, full or partial loss of settlements, infrastructure, agricultural lands, livestock  and loss of human lives, physical injuries and psychological impacts in survivors. Policy Framework Sri Lanka has been a party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCC) ( UNFCCC ) [Accessed 20th February 2026] since 1992.Sri Lanka ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2002  and became a signatory to the Paris Agreement in 2016. Sri Lanka National Policy on Climate Change 2023 ( National Policy on Climate Change )  [Accessed 20th February 2026] which is a significantly updated version of the first National Climate Change Policy 2012, sets the stage for the overall manner in which the country addresses climate change. IT aims to operate in conjunction with other sectoral and national policies. Policies on biodiversity, energy, health, human habitations, agriculture, fisheries and aquaculture,  water resources, infrastructure, industry,  education etc. have  adopted or are in the process of adopting climate change aspects  into their areas of work. Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges Climate change is one of the best examples of the need to include a whole- of- government and whole- of- society approach, without which the impacts of it on biodiversity conservation cannot be addressed. Therefore it is a complex and costly task. This is more so for countries such as Sri Lanka that continue to grapple with the need to promote growth and improve incomes, reduce poverty levels, provide better access to healthcare, decent housing for the majority and improve infrastructure. Convincing the public and policy makers of the far-reaching changes required for transitioning to a low carbon economy is a very serious challenge. Inadequate finances - Even though there is a degree of global support for developing economies, the actual costs of addressing climate change strain the budgets that are already overburdened Legislative gaps- New laws are required for meaningful implementation. This is a slow process. Inadequate technical capacity- Development and implementation of climate change adaptations require some degree of technical knowledge. This is often lacking among those who are in charge of local governance institutions.  Inadequate access to modern technologies is another hindrance . Main Actions Summary: While Sri Lanka's NBSAP aligns with the KMGBF, which is under development, substantial groundwork for KMGBF Target 9 is already being implemented through concrete legal framework, national program ​ me ​ s and projects. Policies, Action Plans, Regulatory Development and Capacity Building : National Policy on Biodiversity (Final Draft 2024, to be approved), National Policy and Strategies on Traditional Knowledge and Practices related to Biodiversity (2020), National Policy on Access to Biological Material and Fair and Equitable Benefit Sharing (2020), ​directly relate to this target ​​ . In addition to the above, The National Agriculture Policy (NAP) of Sri Lanka (Draft) includes a thematic area - Support sustainability in agriculture development through conservation and utilization of natural resources while safeguarding ecosystem services. The Cabinet in 2025 approved the finalization of a new Act for the Protection of New Plant Varieties, aimed at protecting breeders and farmers’ rights. Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance (No 2 of 1937) (FFPO) was amended: FFPO Chapter 469, is the primary legislation in Sri Lanka for the protection and conservation of wildlife, plants, and their habitats. The Ordinance has undergone several amendments to adapt to changing conservation needs. ​A​​amendment Act No. 7 of 2022:​ This act updated the principal enactment to strengthen the enforcement of CITES, allowing for better regulation of international trade in endangered species. It added provisions for appointing ad-hoc committees to provide recommendations on issuing permits under CITES. In August 2025, The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) has urged the President to implement urgent, short-term revisions to the FFPO - significantly increasing fines and penalties. The DWC is in the consultative process to update the FFPO list. ​ The National Herbarium (PDA) of the ​​​ Department ​​​​​​ of National Botanical ​​​ Gardens ​​​​​​ provided data for updating the FFPO and related documents. ​ National Policy on Invasive Alien Species​     ​​​ Strategies and Action Plan ​​(IAS - 2016)​ ​(​ https://env.gov.lk/web/images/downloads/policies/IAS_Policy_English-1.pdf ​)​​ are being implemented: In 2025, the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources prohibited the possession and trade of specific highly invasive fish species, such as the Alligator Gar, Piranha, and Knifefish, to protect local aquatic ecosystems. Forest Ordinance:​​ ​​​  Further revisions to incorporate sustainable, participatory management and private sector involvement, according to the National Forestry Policy is currently undergoing. Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (Amendment) Act, No. 27 of 2023: ​ ​ Provides a strong legal basis for the sustainable management of wild aquatic species. It establishes a comprehensive national framework to prohibit, penalize, and deter ​​ ‘ ​​ Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated ​​ ’ ​​ (IUU) fishing. ​​ National Adaptation Plan (NAP) 2016-2025 developed. The ​ NAP identifies the most vulnerable sectors to the adverse impacts of climate change in Sri Lanka: (a) agriculture; (b) fisheries; (c) water; (d) health; (e) coastal and marine; (f) health; (g) human settlements and infrastructure; (h) ecosystems and biodiversity; (i) tourism and recreation; and (j) industry, energy and transportation. It aims at increasing the country’s resilience of vulnerable communities, areas and sectors by developing policies, strengthening cooperation, promoting institutional setup, mobilizing resources, promoting technology development and transfer, increasing awareness, and building capacity. ​ ​ ( https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/NAP-Sri-Lanka-2016.pdf ​ ) ​​​ ​ In terms of Capacity Building, Sri Lanka has developed comprehensive national guidelines for ecosystem restoration, focusing heavily on mangrove restoration through science-driven, community-based approaches to reverse degradation, with key guidelines launched in 2022 by the Ministry of Environment ( https://www.env.gov.lk/web/images/downloads/biodiversity_division/publications/National_Strategic_Action_Plan_for_Conservation_and_Sustainable_Utilization_of_Mangrove_Ecosyetems_in_Sri_Lanka_2022-2026.pdf ). These frameworks, which include the "National Guidelines for the Restoration of Mangrove Ecosystems" and "National Strategic Action Plan," aim to ensure sustainable, scientific rehabilitation of coastal habitats to support biodiversity and local livelihoods.  National Guidelines for the Restoration of Mangrove Ecosystems of Sri Lanka National Guidelines for the Restoration of Mangrove Ecosystems of Sri Lanka ( https://www.env.gov.lk/web/images/downloads/biodiversity_division/publications/National_Guidelines_for_the_Restoration_of_Mangrove_Ecosystems_of_Sri_Lanka.pdf ) . ‘Lesser-known foods of Sri Lanka’ - an advocacy campaign that aims to tackle the  biodiversity loss and improving access to nutritious food for vulnerable communities across the country. This campaign is directly supported through the Early Action Support (EAS) project, funded by the GEF which plays a critical role in accelerating Sri Lanka’s implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework by integrating biodiversity conservation into national policies and strategies ( https://www.undp.org/srilanka/press-releases/undp-and-wfp-sri-lanka-together-ministry-environment-launch-lesser-known-foods-sri-lanka-campaign-boost-biodiversity-through#:~:text='Lesser%2Dknown%20foods%20of%20Sri%20Lanka'%20is%20an%20advocacy,into%20national%20policies%20and%20strategies . ). The UN Flagship Restoration Award in 2024 recognized Sri Lanka’s viable, lasting solutions towards the restoration of these essential ecosystems which support countless lives and livelihoods across the island. Sri Lanka has also developed the "Forest Restoration Guidebook" (2022) in collaboration with IUCN and the Forest Department, supporting national commitments. ( https://www.pgis.lk/Research/downloads/Guidebook_for_Forest_Restoration_in_Sri_Lanka_2022.pdf ) Project CORE (Climate-smart Opportunities) 2025 - A recent IUCN, Forest Department, and HSBC initiative (2021–2025) in Thanthirimale, Anuradhapura, highlighting practical application, utilizing over 19 native species for restoration. Sustainable use of wild species: promotes sustainable use of wild species through national policies, laws (like Forest Ordinance), focusing on in-situ (reserves) and ex-situ [Department of National Zoological Garden (DNZG) and the Department of National Botanical G ​​ ardens (DNBG)] conservation, integrating biodiversity into sectors such as agriculture and tourism, regulating trade (CITES), and promoting eco-tourism by involving local communities and using scientific tools for habitat management. Key efforts involve habitat protection, controlling illegal trade, research, awareness, and sustainable resource use like timber/firewood and genetic resources for agriculture. A new GEF-funded project (2023-2026)  to assist GoSL to prepare and submit its First Biennial Transparency Report (BTR1), the Second Biennial Transparency Report and Fourth National Communication (BTR2/NC4) to fulfil the obligations under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (Implementing Agency: UNDP, Executing Agency: ​​ ​​ Ministry of Environment) The project addresses data gaps in tracking biodiversity-related NDC goals - Conservation initiatives include in-situ and ex-situ conservation, research on biodiversity, and management of  IAS. ​ ​ The DNZG and DNBG establish and maintain living collections of endangered and economically important wild animals and plants, respectively. The DNBG also has a Plant Tissue Culture laboratory, Molecular Biology laboratory, plant nurseries, and sales centers. The DNBG continuously strengthens the PDA and currently has about 150,000 specimens. Ex-situ conservation is done in 6 botanical gardens ( https://en.botanicgardens.gov.lk/ ) located in different agroclimatic zones. The DNBG has an annual exploration plan and collects and conserves endemic and threatened species. New species are also described. The DNBG also assists the researchers and provides plants for restoration programmes (e.g. Alphonsea hortemsis). The DNBG also conducts research, develops methods, conducts outreach programmes and provides data in developing national databases. The DNZG Sri Lanka (Dehiwala Zoo, Pinnawala, and Ridiyagama) focuses on ex-situ conservation, captive breeding of endangered species (e.g., Banduala Barb, Rusty Spotted Cat, Leopard, primates), veterinary care for wild animals, and animal welfare, including parasite studies. Studies also assess non-captive biodiversity within the zoo, recording over 152 species of fauna and 53 bird species, highlighting its role as an urban wildlife refuge. DNZG has an insurance population for critically endangered species. DNZG conducts scientific research, education, and public awareness programmes, and animal welfare programmes. ​ ​ The National Museum is represented in biodiversity committees, provides inputs on developing biodiversity policies, research, and development on  natural history collections in conservation and utilization plans. Mainstreaming Agrobiodiversity Conservation and ​​ Use ​​​​ in Sri Lankan Agro-ecosystems for Livelihoods and Adaptation to Climate Change , funded by UNEP. ( https://wedocs.unep.org/items/a59b7f3b-2d7a-4aeb-970d-3805c9aa1374 ) was completed in 2017 with the objectives of ensuring that agrobiodiversity in Sri Lanka is optimally conserved and used to meet the challenges of climate change and improve rural livelihoods; increasing the area devoted to sustainably managed agrobiodiversity through use of practices, procedures, institutions, and the improved maintenance and access to new and traditional crops and livestock diversity by local communities; ensuring market and non-market mechanisms are in place that provide farmers with additional rewards from maintenance, to strengthen national strategies, policies and capacity and extension activities on planning for sustainable production of agrobiodiversity products and services, using an ecosystem management approach  ( https://sricat.pdn.ac.lk/index.php/en/projects/climate-change-adaptation-related/183-mainstreaming-agro-biodiversity-conservation-and-use-in-sri-lankan-agro-ecosystems-for-livelihoods-and-adaptation-to-climate-change ; DOI:10.13140/RG.2.2.16479.92323, https://lk.chm-cbd.net/projects/mainstreaming-agrobiodiversity-conservation-and-use-sri-lankan-agro-ecosystems-livelihoods ). Support for Indigenous Peoples & Local Communities (IPLCs): Protects customary sustainable use by indigenous and local communities though collection of forest produces and timber (Extraordinary gazette - No. 1600/18 May 06, 2009 https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/srl133821.pdf ). Sri Lanka’s third NDC places strong emphasis on gender equality and social inclusion, ensuring that climate actions benefit women, youth, Indigenous communities, and persons with disabilities. The policy establishes an effective mechanism to enable ‘Access’ to biological material and sharing of benefits. This will be done by Prior Informed Consent (PIC) and Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) sustainably through the regulation of commercial use, research, other uses, and export of any biological material, including derivatives, components, products, and constructs, as well as associated traditional knowledge, and the use in further research and development in and outside the country. This will be done by Prior Informed Consent (PIC) and Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) sustainably through the regulation of commercial use, research, other uses, and export of any biological material, including derivatives, components, products, and constructs, as well as associated traditional knowledge, and the use in further research and development in and outside the country. Policy covers ‘access’ to any animal, plant, micro-organism, or other material sought for commercial use & other uses of its genetic or biochemical features or related informational value. The National Agriculture Policy (NAP) of Sri Lanka (Draft) includes a thematic area - Support sustainability in agriculture development through conservation and utilization of natural resources while safeguarding ecosystem services. The Cabinet in 2025 approved the finalization of a new Act for the Protection of New Plant Varieties, aimed at establishing a sui generis system to comply with WTO/TRIPS standards. Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance (No 2 of 1937) (FFPO) Amendment Act No. 7 of 2022 strengthens the enforcement of CITES, allowing for better regulation of international trade in endangered species. The DWC is in the consultative process to update the FFPO list. Fisheries and Aquatic Resources Act, No. 2 of 1996, has been formally amended eight times since its enactment. The consistent amendments reflect a legislative effort to address emerging challenges like illegal fishing and to strengthen sustainable fisheries management. The Government of Sri Lanka (GoSL) and GGGI support the delivery of the country’s NDC, SDG targets and GGGI’s 2030 strategy by working across four programmatic solutions on (i) climate action; (ii) sustainable mobility; (iii) renewable energy and energy efficiency; and (iv) forest and mangroves ( https://gggi.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/GGGI-Sri-Lanka-CPF-22.03.04-1.pdf ). Governance Innovation: The launch of a national OECM dialogue ( https://iucn.org/story/202502/national-dialogue-oecms-launches-sri-lanka ) (2024-2025) initiates a process to formally recognize and support community-managed conservation areas. Project on Partnerships and Innovative Financing to Mainstream Biodiversity and Sustainable Land Management in the Wet Climatic Zone of Sri Lanka ( https://www.undp.org/srilanka/projects/innovative-financing-mainstream-biodiversity Project objective: This project aims to integrate biodiversity conservation and sustainable land management practices within the private sector tea and rubber plantations in the wet climate zone of the country. Project period: May 2024 – April 2029, Funded by: Global Environment Facility (GEF)). Sustainable management and use of wild species: Training Manual for Integrating Biodiversity Conservation and Sustainable Use into Land Use Planning in Environmentally Sensitive Areas (ESA) ( https://env.gov.lk/web/images/downloads/environment_planning/publications/esa_manual/english_version.pdf ) was published in 2017 (Enhancing Biodiversity Conservation and Sustenance of Ecosystem services in Environmentally Sensitive Areas (ESA Project), funded by  GEF implemented by the Ministry of Mahaweli Development and Environment with the assistance of UNDP for mainstreaming biodiversity management into development in areas of high conservation significance.) Sustainable Tourism Certification, which has engaged hundreds of businesses and catalyzed millions in biodiversity investment, and a pioneering Payment for Ecosystem Services framework (Launched from 2019 onward. As of June 2025, 37 hotels, 1 destination (Sigiriya), and 204 SMEs are certified. Estimated to have catalyzed USD 4.026 million in biodiversity investments - https://panorama.solutions/en/solution/sri-lankas-national-sustainable-tourism-certification-scheme-promoting-sustainable ). Providing social, economic and environmental benefits for people: sectors like traditional medicine, agriculture, fisheries, and tourism are deeply dependent on wild species. The benefits are substantial, ranging from primary healthcare for 35% of the population relying on Ayurveda to employment for over 150,000 people in fisheries. Protecting and encouraging customary sustainable use by indigenous peoples and local communities: Many initiatives successfully engage those most dependent on biodiversity. Effective models merge community-based systems with formal frameworks. Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs) is an example. OECMs can recognize areas managed by IPLCs for conservation outcomes, even if that is not their primary goal ( https://iucn.org/story/202308/site-level-tool-identifying-other-effective-area-based-conservation-measures-oecms-0 Initiatives like the Veddah Community Upliftment Programme work directly with Sri Lanka's indigenous community to help maintain their cultural identity and traditional knowledge systems, which are linked to sustainable use of forest resources. Support includes handicraft training and facilitating community gatherings. ( https://www.dilmahconservation.org/initiatives/heritage/conserve-vedda-community.html&sa=U&ved=2ahUKEwiBooLx1pySAxUyQkEAHaiNKocQFnoECBcQAg&usg=AOvVaw2Y91okxcWVrsMNXOVaOMgE ). Major Implementation Actions: Clean Sri Lanka & Mangrove Restoration ( https://www.bluegreenlovers.org/2025/01/clean-sri-lanka-building-sustainable.html ): A flagship national programme that includes mangrove restoration as a core project. This work is guided by formal National Guidelines for the Restoration of Mangrove Ecosystems in Sri Lanka, published by the Ministry of Environment in 2021 ( https://www.env.gov.lk/web/images/downloads/biodiversity_division/publications/National_Strategic_Action_Plan_for_Conservation_and_Sustainable_Utilization_of_Mangrove_Ecosyetems_in_Sri_Lanka_2022-2026.pdf ). The guidelines emphasis scientific methods, using native species, and crucially, the active participation of local communities in planning and monitoring to ensure long-term success and benefit-sharing. Blue Swimming Crab Fishery Improvement Project (FIP): Partners: National Fisheries Institute Crab Council (USA), Seafood Exporters’ Association of Sri Lanka, Ministry of Fisheries ( https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/endpovertyinsouthasia/sri-lanka-towards-sustainable-fisheries ). Promotes data-based, participatory management. Uses length-based stock assessments, involves 70+ fishing communities to set sustainable catch levels. Directly aims to make the crab fishery biologically sustainable (Sustains wild species use). Secured premium market access (e.g., US), protecting incomes. In July 2025, the Ministry of Environment held a targeted workshop for over 65 district officials in the Northern Province on "Restoration, Conservation, and Sustainable Use of Blue Carbon Ecosystems." https://nbsapaccelerator.org/news_and_events/sri-lanka-advances-nbsap-implementation-in-northern-province-through-district-level-engagement-on-blue-carbon-ecosystems/ ). This session included field demonstrations on mangrove restoration using the national guidelines and focused on aligning local actions with national biodiversity goals, representing a concrete step in decentralising KMGBF implementation.
Key Challenges Summary: Key challenges encountered Governance & Policy Frameworks: Foundational strengths in law but critical gaps in implementation, monitoring, and inclusive policy. The country is actively engaged in updating its strategies with international support, but the transition from planning to action is crucial Limited Recognition of IPLC Roles: Despite policies, there is no widespread formal mechanism to recognize and support community-managed conservation areas. Implementation & Equity Gaps Data and Monitoring Gaps: Lack of national data on species use, habitat extent, and socio-economic benefits hinder evidence-based decision making. E.g. Ex: while the medicinal plant inventory is critical ( https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006320706001121 ), ongoing monitoring of harvest impacts is needed. Scarcity of data and coordination has been highlighted since 2021- e.g. Background Analytical Study on Availability of Forest Data in Sri Lanka ( https://www.un.org/esa/forests/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Sri_Lanka-Monitoring-Frameworks-Project.pdf ) Critical Financing Gap: • A $190 million biodiversity financing gap (for 2018-2024) ( https://www.undp.org/srilanka/press-releases/9th-regional-dialogue-biodiversity-finance-sri-lanka-features-new-opportunities-narrow-financing-gap-nature-conservation#:~:text=From%20nature%2Dbased%20solutions%20to,government%20between%202018%20and%202024 .) •  Policymakers and financial institutions often merge biodiversity with climate finance. Conservation groups are in the process of developing "bankable" conservation projects. • Current funding is insufficient and unsustainable for long-term needs. Threats to Key Ecosystems: Mangroves and other ecosystems face ongoing pressure from encroachment, pollution, and unregulated development outside protected zones. Need for Robust Benefit-Sharing: Ensuring that economic benefits from sustainable use (e.g., tourism, PES) . Threats to Tradition: loss of elderly knowledge holders and the younger generation moving away from traditional occupations ( https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/2/4/1080 https://www.forestpeoples.org/fileadmin/uploads/fpp/migration/publication/2016/05/fpp-status-trends-trad-occupations-english-web-16.pdf ) Different approaches that may be taken for further implementation Finalize and implement the National Biodiversity Policy and NBSAP (2026- 2030 ), ensuring they explicitly address all aspects of Target 9. Develop and resource a National Monitoring & Information System for wild species and their benefits, building on recent capacity-building initiatives. Enact specific legal and administrative measures to protect customary sustainable use, ensuring active co-creation with IPLCs. Mechanisms such as OECM initiative ( https://iucn.org/story/202502/national-dialogue-oecms-launches-sri-lanka )  to formally recognize and support the customary sustainable use practiced in many case study sites, from community-managed forests to coastal areas. Strengthen the governance and financing framework for sustainable use, addressing bureaucratic hurdles and exploring innovative finance mechanisms like Conservation Trust Funds. Replicate the success of the Mangrove Conservation Project (which provided microloans to 12,000 women ( https://www.seacology.org/project/sri-lanka-mangrove-conservation-project/#:~:text=The%20Sri%20Lanka%20Mangrove%20Conservation,not%20entail%20cutting%20down%20mangroves .) to other ecosystems.
Action Effectiveness Summary: Scientific Case Study on Blue Swimming Crab Fishery- Field study Sept 2017-Nov 2018; published 2023. Assessed overexploited stock. Proposed "sink-source" area-based management (protecting nursery areas, allowing fishing elsewhere) as a tailored, socially acceptable solution. It provides a science-based, culturally informed management model for data-poor, multi-gear small-scale fisheries ( https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocecoaman.2023.106787 ) other related case studies are in the Annexure 9.1.docx
