Main Actions Summary: Policy Framework: A draft National Agriculture Policy (NAP) of Sri Lanka is available and aiming to transform the sector into a modern, sustainable, and competitive industry by 2030. It focused on enhancing productivity, ensuring food safety, promoting eco-friendly operations, and empowering farmers through 10 key thematic areas. https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/SRL226805.pdf Available The National Agriculture Research Policy and Strategy 2018-2027 in Sri Lanka, developed by the Sri Lanka Council for Agricultural Research Policy (SLCARP), aims to align agricultural research, development, and innovation with national development goals. https://www.slcarp.lk/upload/Research-Policy.pdf available In 2024, Sri Lanka initiated its first Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) Investment Plan to combat climate-related threats to food security. The strategy focuses on enhancing resilience, boosting productivity, and attracting private investment to improve agricultural sustainability. Sri Lanka Advances Climate Resilience with First Climate-Smart Agriculture Investment Plan National Fisheries & Aquaculture Policy revised and approved by Cabinet (January 2026). Policy  explicitly include ecosystem approaches and conservation of aquatic biodiversity as part of sustainable resource management. These provisions include assessments before development projects and ecosystem-based planning. https://fisheries.gov.lk/web/images/2019/pdf/National-Policy-090318-English.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com Institutions: Many government national and sectoral institutions are responsible for actions under this target: Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Environment , Ministry of Fisheries, Ministry of Plantation and Community Infrastructure, Department of Agriculture, Department of Agrarian Development, Department of Fisheries & Aquatic Resources, Department of Forest Conservation, Department of Wildlife Conservation, Coast Conservation and Coastal Resource Management Department, National Aquaculture Development Authority of Sri Lanka, Marine Environment Protection Authority, Central Environmental Authority, National Aquatic Resources Research and Development Agency Key Implementation Actions: Examples of actions- Mainstreaming biodiversity into Agriculture and Forestry sectors under Managing together project: Integrating community-Centered ecosystem -based approaches in to Agriculture, Forestry and Tourism sectors  funded through GEF Vi. Mainstreaming biodiversity into agrobiodiversity (FAO), crops, and fisheries – Initiated actions: Under the Technical Cooperation Programme (TCP/RAS/4005), a national gap analysis has been initiated to assess policy, institutional, and practice constraints related to integrating biodiversity into agrobiodiversity, including crop genetic diversity and sustainable fisheries and aquaculture management. GCF Knuckles Project: Strengthening Climate Resilience of Subsistence Farmers and Agricultural Plantation Communities residing in the vulnerable river basins, watershed areas and downstream catchments of the Knuckles Mountain Range: The project focuses on climate-resilient sustainable land and water management, including improved land and water management in upstream catchments to safeguard ecosystem goods and services, rehabilitation of village tanks and irrigation networks, and restoration of forest mosaic landscapes to protect biodiversity and improve watershed functions. Tea Lands :  Netherlands and IUCN tea and coconut agroforestry systems; examples Halgolla Estate (tea) Kurunegala (coconut). This is the example Agroforestry on Degraded Tea and Coconut Plantations (Sri Lankan-Dutch Pilot) (2022/23–March 2025) referred to below. Tea and Rubber Plantations: Partnerships and Innovative Financing to Mainstream Biodiversity and Sustainable Land Management in the Wet Climatic Zone of Sri Lanka (GEF 7) activities on tea and rubber estates on biodiversity conservation, sustainable lands management to establish agroforestry Tea and Rubber plantations - Rainforest Alliance Certification and Forest Stewardship Certification: Rainforest Alliance (RA) and Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certifications are adopted within Sri Lanka’s tea and rubber plantation sector, particularly among members of the Planters’ Association of Ceylon. Rainforest Alliance certification is primarily applied to tea estates . Over 170 have obtained RA certification. FSC certification is mainly applied to rubber plantations. Planters’ Association members manage several hundred estates estimated to cover more than 150,000 hectares, with a significant portion under sustainability certification schemes. However, this figure needs verification.
Progress Summary: Summary of progress Sri Lanka has made some degree of progress in integrating sustainability and biodiversity considerations into production landscapes and seascapes. The current international drive towards biodiversity inclusion in the main sectors that have negative impacts on biodiversity is making the medium and large scale organizations in these sectors to secure certifications, reforestation mosaic landscapes are being planted with native species, to obtain premium prices in the market In fisheries and aquaculture sectors, regulatory frameworks and community-based approaches are expected to contribute to improved awareness of sustainable fisheries. However, progress remains uneven across sectors and regions. While good practices exist, scaling them up and systematically monitoring their impacts towards contribution to biodiversity outcomes remains a significant challenge. Examples of projects implemented: Climate Smart Irrigated Agriculture Project (CSIAP) (2019–31 Dec 2025) Outcome: By the end of 2024, the Climate Smart Irrigated Agriculture Project (CSIAP) demonstrated clear progress toward GBF Target 10 by advancing the sustainable management of irrigated agricultural systems. Cropping intensity increased to 148 %, while crop diversification reached 43 %, indicating more efficient land use and enhanced system resilience. The adoption of Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) practices expanded to approximately 49,000 ha, uptake of sustainable production methods. Capacity-building efforts strengthened long-term sustainability, with 2,163 farmer leaders, including 889 women, trained through the Climate-Smart Agriculture Farmer Training School and cascading CSA practices to about 19,600 farmers across six provinces. In addition, approximately 18,000 trees were established through reforestation and agroforestry interventions, including windbreaks, Kattakaduwa buffer development, and compensated tree planting, supporting sustainable catchment management and landscape resilience. Climate Smart Irrigated Agriculture Project Climate Resilient Integrated Water Management Project (CRIWMP) (2017/18–2024/25) Outcome: The Climate Resilient Integrated Water Management Project (CRIWMP) has advanced sustainable agricultural systems in Sri Lanka’s Dry Zone, directly contributing to KNGBF Target 10. By end‑2023, the project strengthened irrigation and water storage infrastructure across the Malwathu Oya, Mi Oya, and Yan Oya basins, improving year‑round water availability for over 15,000 hectares of farmland and supporting approximately 700,000 smallholder farmers. Climate‑smart practices, including Alternative Wetting and Drying (AWD) in paddy fields, precision irrigation technologies, and drought‑tolerant crop diversification, enhanced water‑use efficiency and cropping intensity (1.6) while reducing ecosystem pressures. Early warning systems and agro‑meteorological advisories promoted climate‑informed agricultural planning. Socio-economic impacts included improved farmer incomes, increased participation of women in adaptive agriculture, and capacity building through climate‑smart training programs, ensuring sustainable and resilient production. Collectively, these outcomes demonstrate CRIWMP’s contribution to sustainable intensification, efficient land and water use, and long-term resilience of agricultural systems. https://www.greenclimate.fund/sites/default/files/document/fp016-50731-annual-performance-report-cy2024-v2.pdf Agroforestry on Degraded Tea and Coconut Plantations (Sri Lankan-Dutch Pilot) (2022/23–March 2025) Outcomes: Development of agroforestry guidelines, monitoring of ecological benefits, and establishment of an agroforestry working group to scale up practices file:///C:/Users/user/Downloads/Guidelines+Agroforestry+in+Sri+Lanka.pdf Ecosystems Conservation and Management Project (ESCAMP) 2016 – 2022 The ESCAMP Project, supported by the World Bank, strengthened landscape-level biodiversity conservation in Sri Lanka by improving protected area management, enhancing ecological connectivity, and mitigating human–wildlife conflict. The project promoted integrated landscape planning and institutional capacity building to ensure sustainable ecosystem management while supporting local livelihoods. Healthy Landscape project (Healthy Landscapes: Managing Agricultural Landscapes in Socio-ecologically Sensitive Areas to Promote Food Security, Well-being and Ecosystem Health) 2019 - 2024 The Healthy Landscapes Project (GEF-6) focused on restoring and sustainably managing socio-ecologically sensitive agricultural landscapes, particularly village tank cascade systems in the Dry Zone. The project enhanced ecosystem services, strengthened agrobiodiversity, and improved food security and community well-being through integrated land and water management approaches. Mainstreaming biodiversity into Agriculture and Forestry sectors under Managing together project (GEF-6) promotes the mainstreaming of biodiversity into agriculture, forestry, and tourism sectors through community-centered, ecosystem-based landscape approaches. Implemented by the Ministry of Environment with UNDP support, the project strengthens cross-sectoral coordination and integrates biodiversity considerations into planning and decision-making processes. (2021-2026) Partnerships and Innovative Financing to Mainstream Biodiversity and Sustainable Land Management in the Wet Climatic Zone of Sri Lanka - GEF 7 (2024–2029). The project aims to integrate biodiversity conservation and sustainable land management practices into the private sector tea and rubber plantation landscapes of the Wet Zone, where about 25% of land is dedicated to these crops and significant endemic biodiversity persists outside formal protected areas. The implementation of the project is currently ongoing. Wilderness and Wildlife Conservation Trust’s (WWCT) ‘Corridors for Conservation’ project has been working in the tea estate landscapes of southern Central Highlands for 10 years working to create partnerships whereby estate companies agree to protect key area of their estates as parts of corridors for wildlife movements. Restoration and widespread community awareness programs are part of this which is aiming to improve overall sustainability of this key agricultural landscape. The above GEF-7 project stems from this ongoing work. Fisheries Dependent Data (FDD) & Fish Aggregating Device (FAD) Programme (NARA) The National Aquatic Resources Research and Development Agency (NARA) is strengthening marine biodiversity conservation through improved fisheries data systems and ecosystem-supportive interventions. The Fisheries Dependent Data (FDD) improvement programme enhances systematic data collection on marine fish landings, generating robust baseline information essential for stock assessment, sustainable harvest limits, and ecosystem-based fisheries management. By improving the accuracy and coverage of fisheries statistics, the initiative supports precautionary management approaches and informed policy decisions aligned with biodiversity conservation objectives. In parallel, the installation and monitoring of Fish Aggregating Devices (FADs) in coastal areas such as Kapparathota and Polhena contribute to stock enhancement and reduced fishing pressure on sensitive reef ecosystems. By strategically aggregating fish stocks, including marine aquarium and edible species, FADs help distribute fishing effort, support community livelihoods, and improve monitoring of species composition and abundance. Collectively, these interventions strengthen ecosystem-based management, enhance resilience of coastal fish populations, and contribute to sustainable use of marine biodiversity in line with national commitments under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). Norway–Sri Lanka Bilateral Cooperation (NARA–IMR Partnership) The bilateral fisheries cooperation between Sri Lanka and Norway, implemented through collaboration between NARA and the Institute of Marine Research (IMR), has significantly strengthened science-based marine resource governance. This partnership enhances biodiversity sustainability through improved fisheries-dependent and research survey-based data systems, standardized sampling methodologies, and strengthened analytical capacity. By building national expertise in stock assessment, ecosystem modelling, and evidence-based regulation, the project supports adaptive and ecosystem-informed fisheries management. Capacity building of Sri Lankan scientists, digitalization of landing data, and development of science-backed regulatory measures contribute to maintaining healthy fish populations and marine ecosystem integrity. The initiative directly supports sustainable fisheries (SDG 14) and CBD priorities by reinforcing national capacity to monitor biodiversity status, manage fishing pressure, and integrate scientific evidence into policy frameworks. Smart & Sustainable Aquaculture (Shrimp Industry Information System – SIIS) FAO–NARA: The FAO-led project “Smart and Sustainable Aquaculture through Effective Biosecurity and Digital Technology,” implemented in collaboration with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the Ministry of Fisheries, Aquatic and Ocean Resources, the National Aquaculture Development Authority (NAQDA), and NARA, advances environmentally responsible aquaculture development in Sri Lanka. The Shrimp Industry Information System (SIIS) the country’s first integrated digital aquaculture platform strengthens sustainability through real-time monitoring of water quality, disease surveillance, traceability, and biosecurity compliance. By integrating digital tools, analytics, and data-driven decision-making, the system reduces disease outbreaks, limits environmental degradation (including effluent impacts), and improves farm-level compliance with ecological standards. Through improved governance, transparency, and early warning mechanisms, the initiative promotes resilient shrimp production systems that safeguard surrounding aquatic ecosystems, protect biodiversity, and support sustainable coastal livelihoods. The project contributes to ecosystem-based aquaculture management, responsible seafood production, and long-term sustainability of aquatic biodiversity in alignment with CBD objectives.

Main Actions Summary: Sri Lanka’s policy and institutional framework is being aligned with Target 12 of the KMGBF by integrating "Fragile Areas" into urban design, promoting ecosystem-based resilience, and enforcing urban nature-based solutions through the UDA and National Physical Planning Department. Key initiatives like the MCUDP and various wetland conservation projects are prioritizing the protection of urban green-blue spaces, as outlined in the NPPP 2050 and related development plans. 1. Policy Framework for Urban Biodiversity Integration National Physical Planning Policy and Plan (NPPP) 2050: Formally gazetted (No. 2127/15, 2019), this plan serves as the macro-level spatial framework. It specifically demarcates "Central Fragile Areas" and "Coastal Fragile Areas" to prevent urban sprawl into biodiversity hotspots, ensuring that high-density development is confined to designated "Developable Areas." Provincial Regional Physical Plans: Currently, regional plans for all nine provinces are being harmonized with NPPP 2050. These plans integrate biodiversity corridors at a provincial scale, ensuring that regional development does not sever ecological connectivity. Mainstreaming Biodiversity in Sectoral Plans: National plans, such as the Sri Lanka Strategic Plan for Tourism (2022–2025) , now include mandatory guidelines for sustainable infrastructure. This ensures that urban tourism development aligns with the conservation of surrounding natural capital. 2. Institutional Framework for Sustainable Urban Governance National Physical Planning Department (NPPD): Operating under the Town and Country Planning Ordinance No. 13 of 1946 , the NPPD utilizes its Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee to ensure that multi-sectoral urban projects (e.g., transport, housing) do not compromise ecological integrity. Urban Development Authority (UDA): As the primary executor of urban land-use policy, the UDA develops Zoning Plans that strictly regulate the conversion of green spaces. By assisting Local Government Authorities (Municipal and Urban Councils, and selected Pradeshiya Sabhas), the UDA decentralizes the enforcement of environmental safeguards in urban centers. Sri Lanka Land Development Corporation (SLLDC): Beyond flood control, the SLLDC acts as a technical custodian for urban waterways and marshes. It maintains the hydraulic and biological health of canal networks, which serve as vital blue-green corridors within the Colombo Metropolitan Area. 3. Regulatory Standards and Environmental Safeguards Planning and Development Regulations (2021): Gazetted under No. 2235/54, these regulations mandate specific Open Space Ratios (OSR) for new developments, directly contributing to the expansion of urban green cover as per Target 12. Western Province Wetland Management Zones: These specialized guidelines provide a legal tier of protection for urban wetlands. They mandate that any urban development within the Western Province must incorporate wetland-sensitive designs , preventing the "in-filling" that leads to biodiversity loss. Integrated Building Approval Procedure: The UDA’s Building Approval Process now functions as a filter for environmental risk. Large-scale urban projects are required to undergo Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA) directed by the Central Environmental Authority (CEA) to evaluate their impact on urban flora and fauna. 4. Flagship Projects for Urban Nature Restoration Metro Colombo Urban Development Project (MCUDP): A landmark initiative that transformed degraded urban areas into functional ecological hubs, most notably the Diyasaru and Beddagana Wetland Parks . These sites serve as "living laboratories" for urban biodiversity. International Conservation Partnerships: Darwin Initiative: Focuses on "Increasing Resilience of Biodiversity and Livelihoods," linking urban poverty reduction with wetland health. GEF Small Grants Programme (Phase 6): Targets socio-ecological resilience, empowering local communities to protect urban biodiversity patches. Colombo Commercial City Development Plan (CCCDP 2019–2030): This plan moves away from traditional "grey" infrastructure by adopting Wetland and Green Space Integration , ensuring that the future commercial heart of Sri Lanka remains a "Wetland City"
Progress Summary: Sri Lanka has made significant strides in integrating biodiversity into urban and territorial planning through the following milestones: Establishment of a Macro-Spatial Framework: The NPPP 2050 was legally gazetted (No. 2127/15, June 2019). This plan serves as the primary instrument for Target 12 by demarcating "Central Fragile Areas" and "Coastal Fragile Areas," effectively restricting urban sprawl into high-biodiversity zones. Decentralized Green Planning: Following the NPPP 2050, regional plans for all nine provinces are currently being formulated to translate national conservation goals into local land-use realities. Digital Transparency in Urban Governance: The Urban Development Authority (UDA) has gazetted and published 60 Urban Development Plans online. This digital availability empowers the public and developers to make informed decisions that respect designated "Conservation Zones" and "Open Spaces." Regulatory Mainstreaming of Biodiversity: Under the UDA Planning and Development Regulations (Gazette No. 2235/54, 2021) , mandatory provisions for Open Space Ratios (OSR) and environmental reservations have been institutionalized, ensuring that urban densification is balanced with accessible green/blue spaces.
Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges: Awareness Gap: There is limited understanding among sub-national institutions and local communities regarding the long-term ecological benefits of the NPPP 2050 , often leading to localized resistance to conservation-based zoning. Fragmented Institutional Implementation: A lack of alignment persists between different government sectors. Fragmented execution often results in infrastructure projects being planned in isolation from the national physical planning boundaries. Limited Inter-sectoral Coordination: Horizontal coordination between urban planners, environmental regulators, and disaster management agencies remains weak, leading to delays in enforcing biodiversity safeguards. Time Lags: The legal procedures for preparing, reviewing, and gazetting plans under the Town and Country Planning Ordinance are time-intensive, sometimes lagging behind the rapid pace of illegal urban land conversions. Approaches for Further Implementation: Initiate targeted awareness programs for the private sector and youth, framing urban biodiversity as an asset for climate resilience and property value. Capacity Building: Upgrade the technical skills of field officers in GIS and Remote Sensing to enable real-time monitoring of "Fragile Areas" and ensure data-driven enforcement. Monitoring & Surveillance: Establish an integrated Digital Monitoring System to identify unauthorized developments or illegal land-filling in protected urban wetlands immediately. Enhance public engagement in the maintenance and protection of urban green spaces, moving toward a community-stewardship model for urban parks. Carrying Capacity Modeling: Integrate advanced technology to model future urban scenarios, identifying the "carrying capacity" of cities to ensure that development does not exceed ecological thresholds.
Action Effectiveness Summary: Case Study : Beddangana Wetland Park Beddagana Wetland Park is located in the Beddagana area of Ethul Kotte, close to Rampart Road, in Sri Jayawardenepura, the administrative capital , Colombo District, western province,  Sri Lanka. This urban ecological sanctuary covers 18 hectares and is part of a larger 1,000-hectares. The Beddagana Wetland Park project was primarily carried out between 2013 and 2016 as a flagship initiative of the Metro Colombo Urban Development Project (MCUDP). Formerly a polluted, abandoned area prone to illegal encroachment, it was restored into a productive wetland. The wetland park serves multiple critical functions beyond recreation. It contributes significantly to flood management in the Metro Colombo region, serves as a critical flood detention area, protecting the administrative capital from extreme rainfall,  providing a refuge for flora and fauna while moderating the temperature of the immediate surroundings. The park acts as an urban "cool island," reducing the local heat island effect and improving air quality for thousands of residents in the surrounding Kotte area. Within the park, there are natural water ponds, marshy areas, seasonally flooding grasslands, and pockets of shrub that support high species diversity, including endemic and threatened animal and plant species. The park is home to a variety of endemic bird species and other wildlife native to Sri Lankan and Asian wetland ecosystems, including butterflies, dragonflies, and various mammals. By managing water flow and preventing stagnant pools through natural filtration, the restored wetland helps in the regulation of water-borne and vector-borne diseases like Dengue. The park features well-designed facilities for visitors and education. It consists of an orientation center, bird-watching tower, bird hides, a floating deck close to Diyawanna Lake, and nature trails through the shrub area. Two main trails offer different experiences: one borders the Diyawanna Oya lake on a raised wooden platform, while the second is a forest trail through wetland woodland. The park has established a butterfly garden rich with host plants and nectar plants, complete with display boards showing life cycles and species descriptions. Beddagana Wetland Center is recognized as the first wetland center built for the wise use of a wetland area integrated into city planning in Sri Lanka, designed and managed by local professionals from the Urban Development Authority. The park offers educational programs, guided tours, workshops for students, and awareness campaigns, successfully increasing public involvement in conservation activities while providing a peaceful retreat for nature lovers in the heart of the busy capital region. Further enhance Eco-tourism and heritage tourism. Progress Summary: Summary of Progress & Outcomes: ● Sri Lanka is party to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and WTO/TRIPS. As a signatory to these agreements/treaties, it is obliged to  provide effective legal mechanisms for both access to genetic/biological resources and benefit sharing, as well as intellectual property protection of the country's biodiversity ( https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3110293 ● Still not a Party to the Nagoya Protocol: Overseas parties have obtained patents and intellectual property rights for some Sri Lankan fauna and  flora, including some traditionally valued Sri Lankan medicinal plants  ( https://archive.roar.media/english/life/environment-wildlife/ending biopiracy-sri-lanka ). ● Sri Lankan is in the process of developing its internal mechanisms/regulations as preparations to sign Nagoya Protocol. Studies have been carried out to assess the benefits and challenges  available for Sri Lanka in ratifying the protocol ( https://journals.sjp.ac.lk/index.php/fesympo/article/view/6533 ). ● The National Policy on ABS (NPABM&FEBS) was passed in 2020 December – it establishes the framework for regulating access to  biological resources, derivatives, and associated traditional knowledge.  It is designed to ensure that benefits derived from these resources are  shared fairly while promoting conservation. The key components  include, Prior Informed Consent (PIC): Required for accessing resources,  Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT): Defines the benefits for the provider and  Material Transfer Agreements (MTA): Required for the transfer of  materials. The Ministry of Environment is  responsible for monitoring the ABS process, including evaluating PIC,  MAT, and MTA. ● Currently relies on existing policies, laws and regulations listed above ( https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3110293 ). ● National Policy and Strategies on Traditional Knowledge (TK) and  Practices related to Biodiversity approved by the cabinet in 2020, aims to document, conserve, and protect Sri Lanka's indigenous knowledge while ensuring equitable benefit-sharing. It seeks to uplift local communities, prevent bio-piracy, and integrate traditional practices into national development. ● However, both ABS and TK national policies do not possess the power to  compel adherence. The absence of binding legal statutes concerning  biological resources, and the associated TK can be identified as a notable deficiency within the legal system. ● Some research has been done to introduce a comprehensive legal  framework related to Traditional Knowledge, under IP law - https://kjms.sljol.info/articles/135/files/6741fbfe8f767.pdf ● While monitoring systems are being developed, currently, there is no  operational national system for monitoring monetary or non-monetary  benefits. ● Capacity gaps are noted as challenges to prevent biopiracy- limited knowledge among some officials identified ( https://journals.sjp.ac.lk/index.php/fesympo/article/view/6533 ). ● Stakeholder dialogue and capacity-building needs are recognized, and the focal point has initiated such programs since 2025. ● FAO Project – from 2024-2026 ( https://www.fao.org/in-action/forest-landscape-restoration-asia/flr-projects/project-detail/enhancing-the-contribution-from-non-timber-forest-products-to-livelihoods-and-food-security-of-local-communities/en#:~:text=To%20strengthen%20capacities%20and%20develop%20mechanisms%20to%20sustainably%20manage%20and%20use%20NTFP . ) Enhancing Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) in Sri Lanka—such as medicinal plants, rattan, and wild fruits—can boost rural incomes, ensure food security, and promote sustainable forest management. Key strategies include developing local capacity, improving value-addition, enhancing market access, and facilitating community-based management to reduce pressure on natural forests. Lead implementing agency: The Department of Forest Conservation The initiative aims to strengthen the sustainable use and management of Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) while contributing to biodiversity conservation and local livelihood improvement in Sri Lanka. Project activities include resource assessments, NTFP resource improvement programmes, and community-based management interventions in selected forest reserves. Target districts include Monaragala (Nilgala), Vavuniya (Nedunkerni Range, Pattide thirinda kulum), Galle (Kanneliya), Matara (Kekunadura),  Mannar (Wedithathiewand), Kurunegala (Galgamuwa), covering savanna, wet evergreen and dry forest ecosystems. Type of NTFPs with tree / plant / animal species of extraction: Areca Nut ( Areca catechu ), Fishtail Palm ( Caryota urens ), Goraka ( Garcinia quaesita ), Jackfruit ( Artocarpus heterophyllus ), Katumberia ( Diospyros melanoxylon ), Bin Kohomba ( Munronia pinnata ), Curry Leaves ( Bergera koenigii ), Gal Siyambala ( Dialium indum ), Walla Patta ( Gyrinops walla ) The project promotes sustainable harvesting practices, habitat-based resource management, and improved monitoring systems.The initiative supports national efforts on sustainable use of biodiversity and enhanced socio-economic benefits from forest ecosystems. ● Protected areas covering over 18% of land area safeguard wild relatives and associated biodiversity. The PGRC conserves over 17,000 accessions representing diverse crop categories, while crop-specific research institutes maintain field gene banks. On-farm conservation continues in traditional systems such as Kandyan homegardens, tank village rice systems, and backyard poultry systems, semi-nomadic cattle and sheep farming systems. These dynamic systems integrate genetic, species, ecosystem, and cultural diversity, providing provisioning, regulatory, supporting, and cultural ecosystem services. ● At present, the gene bank of the Plant Genetic Resources Centre (PGRC) maintains 2,564 traditional rice accessions representing 893 traditional rice varieties.Traditional rice varieties such as Pachchaperumal, Kalu Heenati, Kuruluthuda, and Suwandel possess traits including drought tolerance, submergence tolerance, salinity tolerance, resistance to blast and bacterial leaf blight, and medicinal properties. These traits have contributed significantly to national breeding programs, leading to improved varieties that enabled Sri Lanka to achieve rice self-sufficiency. Similarly, traditional germplasm in millets, pulses ( Vigna spp.), yams ( Dioscorea spp.), banana (Musa spp.), cinnamon ( Cinnamomum zeylanicum ), pepper ( Piper nigrum ), and coconut ( Cocos nucifera ) contains valuable genetic variation for stress tolerance, quality, and adaptation. Many indigenous livestock breeds, such as Thamankaduwa white cattle, Sri Lankan buffalo, Kottukachchiya goat, Jaffna sheep, and village chicken, demonstrate resilience to harsh environments, heat stress, and local diseases, though they often exhibit lower productivity compared to exotic breeds. ● Sri Lanka is particularly rich in crop wild relatives (CWR), including wild rice species such as Oryza nivara , O. rufipogon , O. rhizomatis (endemic), O.granulata and O. eichingeri , which provide resistance to brown plant hopper, grassy stunt virus, drought, submergence, salinity, and iron toxicity. Wild relatives of banana, Vigna, cinnamon, pepper, and sugarcane also serve as reservoirs of adaptive traits. These genetic resources are indispensable for broadening the genetic base of breeding programs and ensuring long-term crop improvement. ● Sri Lanka ratified the BBNJ Agreement (2025), which includes ABS for  marine genetic resources.
Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges: Capacity Gaps: DSI is crucial for accelerating research in Agriculture and Medicine.  A study identified inadequacies in effective quarantine services and limited knowledge among officials as key challenges in implementing ABS, which undermines the state's ability to regulate access and monitor utilization. Developing and enforcing ABS requires significant resources for institutional strengthening, monitoring etc. Balancing Access with Protection: Facilitating bioprospecting for potential national benefit and preventing biopiracy has been challenging. Creating a system that is both attractive to legitimate researchers and protective of national interests is difficult. Some experts express concern that ratifying the Nagoya Protocol could lead to "irreversible damage" to biodiversity, creating a significant policy barrier. Ensuring Community Rights: Integrating the rights and knowledge of indigenous and local communities into a national ABS framework requires careful legal and procedural design to ensure fair and equitable benefit-sharing at the local level. Without being a non-party to the Nagoya Protocol, Sri Lanka has limited access to dedicated international funding, technical support, and capacity building programs under the Protocol, such as those facilitated by Cali fund ( https://www.cbd.int/califund ). Approaches for Further Implementation: Legal: Development of specific regulations and amendments to existing laws if needed (e.g., intellectual property, environmental protection) under ABS and TK Policies as an immediate step. Capacity Building: Develop training programs for relevant officials (customs, quarantine, biodiversity, patent office’s etc) on identifying genetic resources, understanding ABS concepts, and using international databases like the ABS Clearing-House. Parallel sectoral advancement: Ratifying the BBNJ Agreement can be used to build domestic expertise in ABS principles, starting with marine genetic resources, which can later inform a broader terrestrial ABS framework. Pilot Projects & Awareness: Support pilot bioprospecting projects with clear ABS agreements to demonstrate benefits (e.g., research collaboration, technology transfer, capacity building etc). Launch public awareness campaigns on the value of genetic/biological resources and associated TK.

Main Actions Summary: Governance & Cross-Sectoral Planning: Pilot Project for Spatial Planning: A 2016-2017 project integrated biodiversity, ecosystem services, and socio-economic data to identify conservation priorities and inform national development plans ( https://www.cbd.int/jbf/activities/nbsap1/pilotprojects/srilanka ).The pilot provided a methodology for mainstreaming biodiversity into land-use planning. Policy Development: The government is finalizing a new National Biodiversity Policy, Strategy (NBSAP), and a Biodiversity Finance Plan (BioFin) ( https://www.biofin.org/sri-lanka ). Current efforts face integration and data challenges. Policy & Regulatory Tools: Green Public Procurement (GPP): Sri Lanka's National Policy on Green Procurement (NPGP) was approved by the Cabinet in 2023 ( https://www.switch-asia.eu/news/advancing-green-public-procurement-in-sri-lanka/ ). GPP aims to use public spending to drive demand for sustainable products. This aligns public financial flows with sustainability goals. Economic & Financial Alignmen t: The NPGP and related guidelines are key tools for aligning public financial flows with biodiversity and sustainability goals Natural Capital Accounting : Sri Lanka's official biodiversity portal has a dedicated section for tracking progress on integrating biodiversity values into national accounting  ( https://lk.chm-cbd.net/aichi/2-3/biodiversity-values-incorporated-national-accounting-appropriate ). This indicates institutional recognition of the requirement but does not confirm the active production of accounts like the UN SEEA Establishment of Working group for Green Accounting for Forestry Sector, Sustainable Development Division, Ministry of Environment Establishment of National Steering Committee on Green accounting, Ministry of Mahaweli Development and Environment ‘Integration of the Forestry Sector Contribution to the System of National Accounts in Sri Lanka’ (2014) Ministry of Environment and Renewable Energy – provides a complete integration of forest sector environmental values into the national accounting system in Sri Lanka based on the UN SEEA  guidelines It is the first comprehensive study on green accounting in Sri Lanka ( https://journals.sjp.ac.lk/index.php/fesympo/article/view/1030#:~:text=Abstract,survey%20through%20Rapid%20Rural%20Appraisal . ). Development of Green Book for Sri Lanka  - Global Biodiversity Framework Early Action Support (GBF-EAS) Project in Sri Lanka will be implemented by the UNDP in close collaboration with the Ministry of Environment. Under this project, there is a provision to support biodiversity finance solutions that would enable the country to mobilize adequate resources for managing biodiversity assets in a sustainable way. One key output agreed at the project’s National Steering Committee was to support developing a Green Book which aims to guide decision makers on how to assess and evaluate public policy proposals, programmes, and projects incorporating environment asset valuations into the decision-making process. Such guidance would offer a systematic approach to assessing the ‘value for money’ of proposed interventions and helps decision-makers to compare and prioritize different options. It provides a consistent methodology for evaluating the economic, social, and environmental impacts of policy initiatives and infrastructure projects.

Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges Encountered Poor integration of NBSAP targets into development sector agencies led to low achievement (only 19% of priority recommendations from the first NBSAP) ( https://www.efl.lk/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/CBD_Final-1.pdf ). Current policy documents (National Policy, NBSAP, BioFin) are being developed in parallel ( https://www.undp.org/srilanka/blog/conserving-sri-lankas-plant-biodiversity-one-bite-time ; https://gridarendal-website-live.s3.amazonaws.com/production/documents/:s_document/1626/original/SriLanka_brief_final_25.11.24.pdf?1732608731 ; https://iucn.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/gef-id-11944_revised-pif_clean_29-sep-2025.pdf ; https://iki-small-grants.de/k1project/value-sri-lankas-biodiversity-and-ecosystem-services/ ) A significant financing gap of USD 190 million exists for meeting NBSAP targets. The economic crisis has strained public budgets, limiting investments in biodiversity mainstreaming ( https://www.biofin.org/news-and-media/9th-regional-dialogue-biodiversity-finance-sri-lanka-features-new-opportunities ) Data and technical capacity - Use of spatial analysis for conservation is at a preliminary stage. Limited technical capacity for environmental-economic accounting (e.g., SEEA) restricts the ability to quantify biodiversity's monetary and non‑monetary values in decision-making ( https://www.cbd.int/jbf/activities/nbsap1/pilotprojects/srilanka ) Management approaches remain “siloed” without integrated planning, as noted in the Central Highlands project. ( https://iucn.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/gef-id-11944_revised-pif_clean_29-sep-2025.pdf ) Disconnect between climate and biodiversity planning ( https://napglobalnetwork.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/napgn-en-2024-tracking-progress-nbs-eba-nap-processes.pdf ) The National Policy on Biodiversity is still a draft and not yet formally adopted. Regulations to align all public and private financial flows with biodiversity goals are not fully in place. Approaches for Further Implementation Strengthen Institutional Coordination: Establish a high‑level inter‑ministerial committee to oversee the integrated implementation of the National Biodiversity Policy, NBSAP, and BIOFIN. Mandate biodiversity‑inclusive Strategic Environmental Assessments (SEAs) for all major sectoral policies and plans. Scale Up Innovative Finance: Operationalize the Sustainable Finance Roadmap by issuing central bank guidelines for green lending and requiring biodiversity risk disclosures. Develop a pipeline of bankable projects for green bonds and biodiversity credits, leveraging the identified USD 190 million gap. Build Technical Capacity & Data Systems: Invest in natural capital accounting (SEEA) by training statisticians and producing regular ecosystem accounts. Create a centralized spatial data platform to support land‑use planning, building on the 2016‑2017 pilot. Deepen Sectoral Mainstreaming: Develop sector‑specific biodiversity guidelines for agriculture, energy, infrastructure, and tourism, based on the OECD good practices for renewable power ( https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2024/01/mainstreaming-biodiversity-into-renewable-power-infrastructure_b9d9528d/357ac474-en.pdf ). Expand the sustainable tourism certification to cover more value chains and promote it internationally. Enhance Monitoring & Reporting: Regularly publish progress reports to maintain political and public accountability. Leverage International Support: Access the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund (GBFF) and the similar funds for technical and financial assistance. Participate in regional peer‑learning exchanges on biodiversity finance and mainstreaming.
Action Effectiveness Summary: Strengthening the Business & Biodiversity Platform: The Sri Lanka Business and Biodiversity Platform (BSL) was formally rebranded and, in September 2018, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Ministry of Mahaweli Development and Environment. This formalized the public-private partnership recognized business and biodiversity initiative, creating an official channel for the private sector to contribute to national biodiversity targets (NBSAP). By 2018, BSL members had already engaged in over 290 initiatives linked to NBSAP targets since 2010. LIFE Project: Forest Landscape Restoration: n February 2018, BSL, the Forest Department, IUCN, and private companies launched the LIFE Project, a five-year ecological restoration initiative on 12 hectares of degraded rainforest in the Kanneliya Forest Reserve ( https://www.virtusa.com/about/virtusa-foundation/life-project ). The project applied scientific restoration principles and established a Biodiversity Credit Accrual System – a first for Sri Lanka. By 2022, monitoring showed the return of at least 90 new faunal species to the restored area, including butterflies, birds, reptiles, and mammals. The project also created local employment and aimed to remove 3,795 tonnes of CO₂ by 2030. FOCUS 2018: Coastal & Marine Conservation: n May 2018, the FOCUS 2018 project was launched, a collaborative initiative led by the French Embassy, BSL, IUCN, and others to promote Blue Economy and coastal conservation. It included a Declaration of Intent between France and Sri Lanka and focused on the Vakarai-Batticaloa coastline ( https://www.dailymirror.lk/news-features/Focus-A-sustainable-and-innovative-approach-to-protect-the-Ocean/131-150575 ). The project successfully integrated private sector companies through Expressions of Interest, directly linking marine conservation with sustainable economic development. It served as a model for integrated coastal management, aiming to be replicated in other parts of the country. Coastal Zone Management Plan (2018) : The Coastal Zone and Coastal Resource Management Plan 2018 was adopted as a national policy instrument. The plan explicitly mandates the conservation of coastal habitats (like mangroves) and integrates climate adaptation with biodiversity protection, directing sectors like fisheries and tourism towards sustainable practices.

Main Actions Summary: Policy and Institutional Framework for Corporate Biodiversity Responsibility 1. Policy Instruments for Corporate Disclosure and Risk Management National Environment Action Plan (NEAP) 2022–2030: Provides the overarching regulatory roadmap for integrating biodiversity into economic activities. It mandates Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA), ensuring that large-scale business projects assess and mitigate nature-related risks. CBSL Sustainable Finance Roadmap (Updated 2025): The primary instrument for the financial sector. It guides banks, insurance, and capital markets to manage Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) risks, scaling up "green finance" to build a nature-resilient economy. Sri Lanka Green Finance Taxonomy (2022): A classification system that defines "green" investments across key sectors (Agriculture, Forestry, Manufacturing, Tourism). It enables businesses to align their portfolios with biodiversity-positive outcomes and prevents greenwashing. Sri Lanka Financial Reporting Standards (SLFRS S1 & S2): Effective January 2025, these localized standards (aligned with the ISSB) create a mandatory architecture for sustainability and climate disclosures. While currently focused on climate (S2), they provide the foundation for future TNFD-aligned nature and biodiversity reporting. National Framework on Eco-Labelling: Established by the Ministry of Environment, this policy enables consumers to make informed choices by providing verified environmental information at the product level, incentivizing businesses to adopt sustainable production. 2. Institutional Framework for Monitoring and Compliance Ministry of Environment (MoE) & Central Environmental Authority (CEA): The CEA enforces the National Environmental Act, requiring businesses to disclose biodiversity impacts through mandatory EIA/IEE processes and monitoring pollution via Environmental Protection Licences (EPL). Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC): Regulates business activities within or near protected areas, ensuring corporate compliance with the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance. Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE): Acts as a market driver by introducing listing rules that mandate sustainability reporting, pushing public companies toward greater transparency regarding their environmental footprint. Progress Summary: Summary of Progress & Outcomes: Mainstreaming Biodiversity in Tourism : The National Sustainable Tourism Certification Scheme successfully certified 100 SMEs by May 2024. Certified holders reported a 15-20% increase in income , demonstrating that biodiversity-friendly practices create tangible economic value and incentivize private sector investment in sustainable land management. Regulatory Framework for Finance : In partnership with the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL), the Sustainable Finance Roadmap now provides standardized policy guidelines for ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) risk management . This framework covers the banking, capital markets, and insurance sectors, aligning them with global nature-positive financial trends. National Green Taxonomy : The 2022 Sri Lanka Green Finance Taxonomy has been operationalised as a formal classification system. It defines and categorises environmentally sustainable economic activities, providing a mandatory "common language" for large corporations, domestic and foreign investors, and financial product providers to prevent greenwashing and track biodiversity-aligned capital flows.
Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges in Implementation Fiscal Constraints and Private Capital Mobilisation : Ongoing fiscal tightening has limited the government's ability to provide direct subsidies or tax incentives. This places a greater burden on the private sector to lead the mobilisation of green capital and nature-positive investments independently. Inter-sectoral Coordination : While frameworks exist, implementing finance solutions across disparate sectors (banking, tourism, agriculture) remains complex. While initial dialogues have occurred, deep institutional integration —where biodiversity data flows seamlessly between environmental agencies and financial institutions—is still in its early stages. Verification and Impact Gaps : A significant challenge remains in the systematic monitoring of environmental outcomes. Without robust data to link financial investments to actual on-the-ground biodiversity recovery, it remains difficult to refine evidence-based policies or ensure corporate accountability. Strategic Approaches for Further Implementation Operationalizing Green Lending : Strengthen banking sector integration by developing specific green lending products and nature-related ESG risk assessment frameworks. This includes providing banks with clear, science-based definitions of "biodiversity-positive" activities to simplify credit appraisals. Revenue Streams via PES : Implement the Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) scheme, particularly within the power generation and water sectors. This will create self-sustaining revenue streams where businesses pay for the "upstream" biodiversity protection that secures their water and energy supplies. ( https://www.biofin.org/news-and-media/revitalizing-payment-ecosystem-services-pes-sri-lanka-building-capacity-future Coordinated Capacity Development : Address the pervasive capacity gaps across financial institutions, government bodies, and CSOs through a unified national training program . This will ensure all stakeholders can interpret and apply complex biodiversity disclosure standards like SLFRS S1 & S2 . Blended Finance Innovation : Develop Blended Finance Instruments that combine GEF grants, philanthropic contributions, and commercial bank loans. By using "concessional" capital to de-risk projects, Sri Lanka can attract large-scale private investment for landscape-level conservation and community-led biodiversity initiatives.

Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges: Despite progress, Sri Lanka faces steep challenges in scaling implementation and changing deep-seated behaviors. Weak Waste Management Systems & Infrastructure: A fundamental obstacle is the lack of effective collection and processing systems. Include treatment & final disposal facilities .Reports note common practices of street dumping, open burning, and improper use of dump sites, which lead to public health risks like dengue outbreaks ( https://unitar.org/about/news-stories/stories/raising-awareness-sustainable-consumption-sri-lanka ). Entrenched Public Habits and Low Awareness: Shifting consumer behavior is difficult. There is a noted public comfort with littering and a lack of concern, alongside limited understanding of sustainable alternatives ( https://unitar.org/about/news-stories/stories/raising-awareness-sustainable-consumption-sri-lanka ). Political and Institutional Barriers: The political landscape can be divided on environmental issues. A lack of consistent political will and powerful economic interests (e.g., landowners profiting from waste dumping) can stall systemic reforms ( https://unitar.org/about/news-stories/stories/raising-awareness-sustainable-consumption-sri-lanka ). Limitations of Project-Based Approaches: Many successes, like the Riviera Resort biogas unit, remain isolated pilots. Scaling these to a national level requires sustained funding, technical support, and a supportive regulatory environment that is often lacking ( https://www.eeas.europa.eu/node/47571_en ). Approaches for Further Implementation: Strengthen and enforce regulations; scale economic instruments. Finalize and enforce the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) scheme for plastics. Expand the Green Public Procurement policy to cover more government spending ( https://www.scp.env.gov.lk/home.php ). Prioritize investment in circular economy infrastructure. Develop centralized composting and material recovery facilities. Create financial incentives (low-interest loans, grants) for businesses and municipalities to adopt technologies like biogas.   ( https://www.eeas.europa.eu/node/47571_en ). Foster community ownership and empower local champions. Support and replicate community-driven models like the Colombo Flea Market. Launch nationwide "Clean Sri Lanka" type campaigns that combine clean-ups with education on waste segregation. Mainstream SCP into education and other policy sectors. Integrate SCP modules into school and university curricula. Ensure SCP measures are explicitly included and funded in the implementation plans for Sri Lanka's updated climate targets (NDC 3.0) ( https://www.iges.or.jp/en/pub/integrating-sustainable-consumption-and-production-scp-and-climate-change-policy-strategic/en ) . Main Actions Summary: The main actions taken toward implementing the National Policy on Biosafety and fulfilling obligations under the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety include: Policy Adoption: Sri Lanka's National Policy on Biosafety was approved by the Cabinet of Ministers in 2005 , forming part of the broader National Biosafety Framework (NBF) of Sri Lanka developed to ensure the safe use of modern biotechnology, aligning with the Cartegena Protocol on Biosafety that Sri Lanka ratified in 2004. Preparation of a Biosafety Act : The National Biosafety Framework (NBF) of Sri Lanka was developed in 2005, which included drafting a specific Biosafety Act to regulate Living Modified Organisms (LMOs) / Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs). A draft of the Biosafety Act was created in 2014, but it remained pending enactment for several years due to capacity limitations. As part of a Global Environment Facility (GEF) project implemented by the FAO and the Ministry of Environment (2017–2023), the draft Biosafety Act was revised to strengthen the regulatory system.The draft stage  Biosafety Act aims to provide the legal authority to regulate the import, handling, and use of Living Modified Organisms (LMOs) and Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) in Sri Lanka. Interim Regulations/ Regulatory Development: In the absence of a comprehensive Act, Sri Lanka uses the Food (Control of Import, Labeling, and Sale of Genetically Modified Foods) Regulations of 2006 (Specific regulations have been enacted under existing and its 2023 amendment) under the Food Act No. 26 of 1980. This amendment raised the threshold for mandatory GMO labeling from 0.5% to 0.9%. The primary legal tool used to manage the entry of plants and plant-related organisms is the Plant Protection Act, No. 35 of 1999. Act gives the Director-General of Agriculture the power to regulate any "organism" that could be harmful to plant health. The NPQS classifies GMOs as potential "quarantine risks." In the Import Permit, required to provide a certificate. Institutional Coordination: Ministry of Environment in Sri Lanka acts as the national focal point and Biodiversity Secretariat of the Ministry coordinates biosafety-related activities across multiple agencies. As per the draft Act, the Central Environmental Authority has been identified as the National Competent Authority for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of this act. Risk Assessment Processes: Procedures for scientific risk assessment are embedded in regulations like the Control of Pesticides Act and the GM Food Regulation. Draft documents were developed by the FAO-GEF project mentioned above. Border Control Mechanisms: Sri Lanka Customs, in coordination with other technical agencies (e.g., Plant Quarantine, Department of Animal Production and Health), screens imports, though challenges remain due to HS code classifications for LMOs/GMOs. International Compliance: Sri Lanka is a party to key agreements including the Cartagena Protocol, CBD, WTO-SPS, and IPPC, and has submitted National Reports on implementation.
Progress Summary: Summary of Progress & Outcomes: A National Biosafety Policy (2005) provides a clear policy direction. A Draft Biosafety Act has been developed to create a comprehensive legal framework, and it is at t he Legal Draftsman’s Department, awaiting approvals from the Attorney General’s Department, Cabinet, and Parliament. Sectoral regulations under food and plant protection provide interim regulatory controls. A functioning, though complex, multi-agency system involving Customs, Agriculture, Health, and Environment ministries regulates transboundary movement and domestic use. As part of a Global Environment Facility (GEF) project implemented by the FAO and the Ministry of Environment (2017–2023) on Implementation of the National Biosafety Framework in accordance with the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, a National Referral Lab at the Agricultural Biotechnology Center of the University of Peradeniya, two National testing labs, one at the National Plant Quarantine Service of the Department of Agriculture and the other at the Industrial Technology Institute for detection and identification of LMO/GMO were developed and the staff was trained in international and national level. Under the same project, following materials are prepared in consultation with all the stakeholders handed over to the Biodiversity Secretariat of the  Ministry of Environment Annexure 17.1.docx Risk assessment capability has been demonstrated in specific cases (e.g. a specific risk assessment was conducted for the release of Wolbachia -infected mosquitoes for dengue control and two are two other products are in the process – a bio larvicide and a fabric dye produced through a GM organism ). Sri Lanka is an active Party to the Cartagena Protocol and uses the Biosafety Clearinghouse.
Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges: Legislative Gap: The absence of an enacted Biosafety Act is the primary obstacle. It leaves the system fragmented and without a clear National Competent Authority with overarching powers. Institutional Fragmentation: Over 10 agencies operate under different laws with overlapping, uncoordinated, and sometimes conflicting mandates (e.g., for GM food imports, feed import, seed/planting material import). Technical & Resource Constraints: Lack of a dedicated, well-funded biosafety authority/competent authority; insufficient human resources and technical expertise for risk assessment and monitoring, new laboratory testing and identification methods (e.g.: digital PCR). Awareness and acceptance: Even though many awareness programs have been conducted under two national projects, more to be done to convey the scientific knowledge among all the stakeholders. Systemic Weaknesses: Customs controls are hindered as LMOs are not explicitly recognized in HS Codes. Public awareness and participation mechanisms are underdeveloped. Emergency response measures are not adequately addressed. Approaches for Further Implementation: Priority Legislative Action: Finalize, revise addressing identified gaps, and enact the Biosafety Act to establish a legally empowered National Competent Authority. Strengthen Institutional Framework: Create a clear administrative structure for the biosafety authority with secure funding, technical cadres, and a strong mandate to coordinate all relevant agencies. Capacity Building: Invest in human resource development, expert committees, and accredited laboratory networks for risk assessment and compliance monitoring. System Integration: Amend existing laws (Plant Protection, Seed, Food, etc.) to align with the biosafety policy and improve HS Code recognition for LMOs at borders. Public Engagement: Implement a structured public awareness, education, and participation strategy to build informed stakeholder dialogue.
Action Effectiveness Summary: Case 1: Regulation of GM Food Imports: Under the Food (Control of GM Foods) Regulation 2006 (amended in 2023) , an application procedure exists. While no formal applications were received up to 2025, the regulation provides a legal basis for the Chief Food Authority to require declarations (e.g., from milk powder importers on non-GM feed), demonstrating the activation of precautionary controls. Case 2: Risk Assessment for Biocontrol: The collaborative project led by the Ministry of Health for the phased release of Wolbachia -infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes for dengue control involved a dedicated scientific risk assessment prior to approval. This shows the application of the risk assessment principle in a contained environmental release. Case 3: Inter-Agency Border Control: For suspected GM consignments, Sri Lanka Customs requests clearance certificates from multiple technical authorities (Plant Quarantine, Animal Production and Health). The denial of several requests for GM maize and soybean imports (as recorded in the 2018 report) illustrates that the existing, albeit complex, system can prevent unauthorized entry. Main Actions Summary: Target 18 the focus must shift from general conservation funding to the identification and elimination of harmful subsidies (reducing them by at least $500 billion per year globally by 2030) and the scaling up of positive incentives for biodiversity. 1. Reform of Harmful Incentives & Market-Based Instruments Policy Frameworks: National Environmental Policy (2022) promotes market-based environmental instruments, polluter-pays principle, and sustainable financing. National Policy on Biodiversity 2024 (draft). Green Finance Roadmap of Sri Lanka (2019) promotes green bonds, sustainability-linked finance, and biodiversity-positive investments, which linked to Paris Agreement and SDGs Environmental Conservation Levy Act No. 26 of 2008 (commenced 6 June 2008) establishes a legislative framework for imposing a targeted levy on certain goods, services, and ownership of specified items that are likely to adversely affect the environment. Regulations and Action Plans National Environmental Action Plan (2022-2030) Rationalizing Ecosystem Access Fees: Based on the 2025 report ‘Getting the Price Right’ by CSF, Sri Lanka has introduced higher seasonal entry fees for Category 1 National Parks (e.g., Yala). This move shifts the burden from public state funding to a "User-Pays" model , ensuring that tourism revenue more accurately reflects the true cost of conservation and ecosystem maintenance. ( https://www.csf-asia.org/getting-the-price-right-rationalizing-park-entry-fees-and-the-case-of-yala-national-park/ ). Carbon-Based Taxation & Vehicle Electrification: In line with shifting away from fossil-fuel dependencies, the Revised Carbon (Green) Tax was operationalized. This mechanism creates a disincentive for internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles while providing tax exemptions for electric vehicles , effectively redirecting private capital toward lower-impact technologies. Development of Positive Incentive Frameworks National Policy on Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES): Currently under development, this framework aims to formalize schemes where land managers are rewarded for maintaining biodiversity. Pilot programs are already active in watershed protection and mangrove conservation , transitioning from a "command-and-control" approach to a "reward-for-service" model. Sustainable Finance Roadmap 2.0 (2025-2029): Led by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka , this roadmap address the sustainable financing at the global level and to address domestic market development and stakeholder demand in line with the Central Bank objectives of price and financial system stability. Innovative Financing & Debt Restructuring Exploratory work towards Debt-for-Nature Swap (2023–2024) — a Debt-for-Nature Swap (DFNS) as an innovative financing mechanism to redirect external debt obligations toward climate action, renewable energy, and environmental conservation was explored, but a formal DFNS agreement has not yet been finalized as of early 2026. The initiative remains a core part of the National Climate Finance Strategy (2025–2030) , launched in October 2025, which sees it as a tool to bridge the estimated financing gap needed for Sri Lanka's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) by 2030. The Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN): Sri Lanka is actively utilizing the UNDP BIOFIN methodology to identify the "finance gap" and develop domestic resource mobilization strategies that reduce reliance on biodiversity-harmful subsidies. Regulatory & Institutional Strengthening Central Bank & Treasury Incentives: Direct financial incentives have been introduced to encourage Green Financing, providing preferential treatment for projects that demonstrate a net-positive impact on biodiversity. Interim & Sectoral Mechanisms: In the absence of a singular overarching biodiversity finance law, the state has utilized Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) and donor-supported Biodiversity Trust Funds to manage protected area financing efficiently. Lead Agency Coordination: The Ministry of Finance and Central Bank with the MoE in partnership, has established a multi-sectoral framework to ensure that economic policies do not inadvertently provide incentives that lead to habitat destruction. Key Partners: Central Environmental Authority (CEA) Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) Department of Forest Conservation Ministry of Finance Central Bank of Sri Lanka Climate Change Secretariat NGOs (IUCN Sri Lanka, WNPS, SLYCAN Trust) Private sector & donor agencies (GEF, UNDP, World Bank) Ministry of Environment Key Outcomes of Major Programs (2022–2025) Mangrove PES Pilots: Successfully demonstrated the viability of community-led conservation through direct financial incentives. Revenue Enhancement: The implementation of evidence-based fee structures in National Parks has begun to bridge the funding gap for the Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) . Green Bond Frameworks: Established the groundwork for sovereign and corporate green bonds to fund large-scale nature restoration. Progress Summary: Summary of Progress Sri Lanka has transitioned from conceptual planning to the early implementation of diverse biodiversity finance mechanisms: Expansion of Economic Instruments: Successfully introduced pilot Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) for watershed and mangrove protection. This is complemented by evidence-based conservation fees in high-demand parks like Yala to better reflect ecological costs. Green Finance Integration: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka has well-anchored its Green Finance Taxonomy and Sustainable Finance Roadmap 2.0 into the banking sector, promoting biodiversity-positive credit lines. Resource Mobilization: Secured $5.8 million from the Kunming Biodiversity Fund (KBF) in late 2025 to strengthen biodiversity integration in agrifood systems, specifically addressing KMGBF targets. Strategic Planning: The National Biodiversity Strategic Action Plan (NBSAP 2026–2030) and a dedicated Biodiversity Finance Plan are currently under stakeholder consultation as of October 2025. Debt-for-Nature (DFN) Scoping: While a formal swap has not yet closed, DFN mechanisms are now a central pillar of the National Climate Strategy 2025 to bridge the estimated $190 million biodiversity finance gap.
Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges Policy & Legislative Gaps: There is still no binding national legislation for PES or a fully operational national biodiversity finance policy. Institutional Fragmentation: Coordination remains inconsistent between the Ministry of Environment, Ministry of Finance, and sectoral agencies, leading to fragmented implementation of the "polluter-pays" principle. A persistent lack of standardized biodiversity valuation data makes it difficult to calculate the "bankability" of nature projects for private investors. Socio-Economic Trade-offs: The 2026 economic outlook focuses heavily on industrial recovery (projected 4.6% growth), which often creates competing interests with conservation goals. Nascent Market Awareness: Bankers and corporate entities still largely conflate "biodiversity finance" with "climate finance," often neglecting nature-based solutions in favor of renewable energy projects. New Approaches for Further Implementation Legislative Formalization: Drafting an overarching National Biodiversity Policy (identified as a priority task in February 2026) to provide a legal basis for sustainable utilization and resource mobilization. Innovative Debt Instruments: Moving toward Sovereign Green Bonds and specialized "Blue Bonds" for marine conservation as part of post-debt-restructuring financial strategies. Biodiversity Credits & Markets: Exploring the integration of biodiversity credits into the national carbon market to incentivize private-sector forest and wetland restoration. Digital Monitoring: Implementing digital tools and citizen science platforms (Action 18.1) to monitor the impact of financial investments in real-time. Public-Private-Community Partnerships: Scaling "Community-led PES" models where rural livelihoods are directly tied to the health of local ecosystems, ensuring a "just transition" from harmful subsidies.
Action Effectiveness Summary: Examples/ case Studies Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) Talawakelle Tea Estates Pilot (2024–2025): Identified as a high-potential pilot site by UNDP BIOFIN, this study explores a PES model within the plantation sector. It focuses on rewarding tea estates for watershed management, soil conservation, and forest connectivity. The goal is to move from traditional corporate responsibility toward a business-driven model where conservation generates verifiable financial credits. Vidullanka PLC Mini-Hydro Catchment (2022–2025): One of the first functional PES pilots in Sri Lanka, where a private energy provider partnered with IUCN and BIOFIN to fund catchment rehabilitation. The project links hydro-power generation with the health of the upstream watershed, establishing a direct financial flow for ecosystem maintenance. Mangrove PES Pilot Programme - Communities receive financial incentives to protect mangrove ecosystems benefiting fisheries and coastal protection Modelling soil erosion and hydropower linkages of Rantambe reservoir, Sri Lanka: towards payments for ecosystem services – A study that explored the mechanisms available for implementing a payment for ecosystem service were analysed against the assessment of the impact of soil erosion on reservoir sedimentation and the economic losses. Reforming Harmful Incentives: The Fertilizer Subsidy Transition Gradual Reform of Chemical Subsidies (2023–2025): Following the severe yield impacts of the 2021 sudden import ban (which saw maize yields drop by 68% and average yields by 52%), the government adopted a phased approach. A new "Fertilizer Cash Grant" model replaces blanket chemical subsidies, allowing farmers to choose organic alternatives and reducing the direct state incentive for chemical overuse. Main Actions Summary: The main actions taken towards implementing include, Policy Framework for Resource Mobilization National Environmental Policy (NEP) Alignment: The NEP provides the foundational "vision for sustainability," legally anchoring market-based instruments and Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) . It emphasizes intergenerational equity, ensuring that biodiversity financing is not a one-time grant but a sustainable, long-term flow. Sustainable Finance Roadmap 2.0 (2025–2029): Adopted by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) in 2025 with support from the EU (ACSIIS Programme), this roadmap is the primary driver for private sector resource mobilization . It integrates ESG disclosures and green lending frameworks to shift commercial capital toward biodiversity-positive outcomes. National Climate Finance Strategy (2025–2030): Approved by the Cabinet on September 8, 2025, this strategy integrates Natural Capital Accounting and "Nature-Positive" instruments, such as Blue Bonds and Green Revolving Funds , to bridge the national biodiversity finance gap. Strategic Regulations and Innovative Action Plans BIOFIN Sri Lanka Finance Solutions: Since 2017, BIOFIN has moved from planning to execution, successfully implementing: Sustainable Tourism Certification: A national system that redirects tourism revenue into conservation. Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES): Active pilots in the hydropower sector that internalize the cost of watershed protection. Sri Lanka Coral Reef Initiative (SLCRI) & CORALL Trust Fund: Established in late 2025, the CORALL Conservation Trust Fund (CCTF) acts as a dedicated financial vehicle. It utilized an initial LKR 97 million grant from the Global Fund for Coral Reefs (GFCR) to leverage additional private investment for marine "refugia." Carbon & Biodiversity Credits: Initiatives are underway to develop voluntary Biodiversity Credit markets, allowing the private sector to invest in measurable nature restoration alongside carbon offsetting. Sustainable Tourism Certification System (adopted nationally in 2019) Interim Regulatory Development & Standards In the absence of a standalone Biodiversity Finance Act, Sri Lanka is utilizing a "Modular Regulatory Approach": TNFD-Aligned Disclosures: Encouraging financial institutions to adopt the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) framework to identify and mitigate nature-related risks in their portfolios. Voluntary Green Standards: The Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) are implementing voluntary standards for Green and Sustainability Bonds to attract international impact investors. Green Book for Sri Lanka (NPD/MoE) Institutional Framework & Coordination Lead Agencies: A lead structure comprising the Ministry of Environment (Technical), Ministry of Finance (Fiscal), and Central Bank (Monetary) considers how biodiversity can be treated as a core economic asset. The National Planning Department also provides technical inputs. Key Implementation Partners: Collaborative efforts include IUCN Sri Lanka for technical valuation, Environmental Foundation Ltd. (EFL) for trust fund governance, and the Sri Lanka Banks’ Association (SLBA) for private sector uptake. Multilateral Coordination: The CBSL Sustainable Finance Stakeholder Platform serves as a unified hub for regulators and donor agencies (UNDP, EU, World Bank) to align biodiversity-related financial flows. Major programmes/ projects/ activities: Conservation of Reefs for All Lives and Livelihoods (CORALL) – CCTF The CORALL Conservation Trust Fund (CCTF) is the initiative's flagship financing mechanism, formally established on 31 December 2025 to ensure long-term, sustainable funding beyond the project's lifespan. Funding sources include tourism levies, eco-enterprise revenue, and voluntary contributions. It operates as a revolving trust fund model, reinvesting returns into coral seascapes. Action Effectiveness Summary: Example 1: Sustainable Tourism Certification (BIOFIN) Background and Establishment The National Sustainable Tourism Certification Scheme (NSTCS) was launched in 2018 by the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) in collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) through the Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN). The partnership was formalized following a workshop held in May 2018 in Colombo involving all key tourism stakeholders to discuss a roadmap for establishing the scheme. To ensure technical compliance with internationally recognized certification schemes and gain international recognition, SLTDA signed a memorandum of understanding with the Global Sustainable Tourism Council (GSTC), adapting their guidelines for Sri Lanka's scheme. Implementation Phases Phase 1: Accommodation Sector (2018-2019) The pilot project initially targeted the accommodation sector, but faced challenges as Sri Lanka had no trained auditors for the GSTC certification process. SLTDA worked with BIOFIN to arrange GSTC trainers who conducted a four-day training programme for officers from provincial councils, the Ministry of Tourism, universities, and other institutions, resulting in 42 successfully trained officers. The pilot phase for the accommodation sector was successfully completed in 2019. Phase 2: Destination Certification (2020-2021) Despite challenges including the 2019 Easter bombings, a government change, and the COVID-19 pandemic, SLTDA allocated LKR 12 million (US$33,000) in 2020 to advance the sustainable destination certification scheme in partnership with BIOFIN. Nine destinations across the country were targeted for Sustainable Destination Certifications, with Sigiriya identified as the first site to achieve certification. (source) Phase 2: SME Expansion (2023-Present) In 2023, a call for applications was opened for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in the tourism sector, with a strong emphasis on women entrepreneurs. Over 100 SMEs in the tourism sector were awarded certifications in May 2024 in the presence of high-level dignitaries from the tourism and development sectors. By 2025, UNDP through BIOFIN had certified 200 small and medium enterprises under Sri Lanka's NSTC scheme, with businesses reporting income increases of 15-20 percent driven by improved visibility on international travel platforms such as Booking.com. Example 2: CORALL Conservation Trust Fund (2025) A revolving conservation financing mechanism funding coral reef resilience and coastal livelihoods in Puttalam, Trincomalee, and Batticaloa. The Trust Deed was formally signed on December 31, 2025, by Environment Foundation (Guarantee) Limited (EFL) as Settlor together with inaugural trustees, officially establishing Sri Lanka's first dedicated coral reef conservation trust fund. The fund was publicly announced on World Fisheries Day, November 22, 2025, at the "Aqua Planet" exhibition in Colombo.
