Main Actions Summary: Towards this target there have been several initiatives and actions, namely various capacity building initiatives; technology uptake, use and transfer; as well as scientific and technical cooperation initiatives. Sri Lanka's primary biodiversity policies mention capacity building as a supporting element; however, the following policies and frameworks have dedicated components specifically for strengthening human, institutional, and technical capabilities: The NBSAP 2016-2022: contains a dedicated chapter (Chapter 4) titled "Needs for Implementation" that includes a specific Plan for Capacity Development. It targets 12 national objectives, with the first explicitly focused on building capacity for understanding indigenous biodiversity. National Policy on Invasive Alien Species (2016): has "Capacity Development" as one of its five core policy statement sections. It mandates the improvement of both human and physical resources for risk assessment and early warning systems, as well as strengthening inspection capacity at entry points. National Policy on Biosafety implemented alongside the "National Biosafety Framework," includes a focused project for Strengthening Policy, Institutional and Regulatory Frameworks. It specifically aims to develop technical capacity for the detection and identification of Living Modified Organisms (LMOs). National Policy on Access to Biological Material and Fair and Equitable Benefit Sharing: states that building in-country capacity within institutions and individuals is a primary requirement to operationalize the national regime for benefit sharing and technology transfer. National Policy on Biodiversity (Final Draft): aims to “facilitate capacity building by disseminating and developing required knowledge, skills, will and the unity”. Biodiversity Finance Plan (BioFin): contains capacity‑building components, e.g. training on performance‑based budgeting for biodiversity investment. In addition, there have been several national level research centres set up, as well as those linked to the universities. A conducive environment has been created to enable the private sector, as well as NGOs to set up research centres as well, some of which have a very focused approach. Towards establishing technology and science cooperation partnerships/programmes: there have been some projects carried out, mostly with bilateral or multilateral funding support, details in part 3.

Key Challenges Summary: Key Challenges Encountered Lack of a Dedicated National Action Plan: Capacity-building is scattered across documents rather than being a focused, implemented strategy. Initiatives are often tied to short-term international projects (e.g., BioFin, individual conservation projects). This risks lack of sustainability, duplication, and gaps once projects conclude. Insufficient Mainstreaming of Inclusivity: While gender and community participation are mentioned in projects, there is no clear evidence of a systematic national assessment or strategy to address the specific capacity needs of Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women, youth, and persons with disabilities for biodiversity. Gaps in Comprehensive Capacity Needs Assessment: The strong financial needs assessment (BioFin) has not been mirrored by a broader National Capacity Needs Self-Assessment that evaluates functional, technical, and institutional capacities across all sectors relevant to biodiversity. Limited Documentation of Technology Transfer: There is little documented evidence of active, national-scale programmes for developing or transferring technology (e.g., monitoring tech, indigenous knowledge systems) or fostering joint scientific research. Approaches for Further Implementation Develop and Resource a Unified Action Plan: Formulate a National Capacity Development, Technology Transfer, and Scientific Cooperation Action Plan for biodiversity. This plan should be costed, aligned with the NBSAP, and integrated into national development budgeting. Conduct a Comprehensive Capacity Needs Assessment: Launch a new National Capacity Needs Self-Assessment (NCSA) process. This should build on BioFin's financial data to evaluate technical, institutional, and individual capacity gaps across all relevant ministries and stakeholders. Systematize Inclusive Participation: Mandate and fund a national assessment of the capacity needs of specific groups (IPLCs, women, youth, persons with disabilities). Integrate findings into all biodiversity planning and establish clear mechanisms for their equitable participation in decision-making and benefits. Catalyze Technology and Innovation Partnerships: Establish a national platform to connect research institutions (e.g., universities) with government agencies and communities to identify technology needs and foster South-South and triangular cooperation in areas like remote sensing, DNA barcoding, or sustainable agriculture. Strengthen Monitoring and Reporting: Establish a national mechanism to systematically track and report on capacity-building activities, technology partnerships, and inclusive participation. This will improve accountability and provide clearer data for future global reporting
Action Effectiveness Summary: A dedicated project (Sept 2019 – Aug 2023) of the Sri Lanka Forest Department implemented from September 2019 to August 2023 by IUCN Sri Lanka and the International Union of Forest Research Organizations (IUFRO), trained over 400 field forest officers across all 23 forest divisions in Forest Landscape Restoration (FLR) techniques. This project developed a critical mass of practitioners and embedded FLR into the national forestry training institute curriculum ( https://www.iufro.org/spdc-capacity-building-flr-sri_lanka ). The project's training materials and curriculum were institutionalized within the Sri Lanka Forestry Training Institute, ensuring long-term sustainability of capacity-building efforts. It supported Sri Lanka's commitment to the Bonn Challenge, a global effort to restore degraded land. SMART Patrolling : The DWC has integrated the Spatial Monitoring and Reporting Tool (SMART) , an open-source platform that uses a mobile app ( SMART Mobile ) on smartphones to record georeferenced data. Progress Summary: There have been extensive communication and awareness creation efforts on biodiversity conservation and responsible use in Sri Lanka over the past 10 years. The lead agencies with portfolios that relate to biodiversity (BDS, various other divisions within the MoE, the DWC, the FD, CCD, MEPA etc.) have regular awareness creation programmes for school children, public and public officials. Each of these agencies carry out around 20 to 30 programmes per year (some monthly, some quarterly and others annually). The NBSAP had an action under Target 2 to publicize guidelines to reduce the impact of tourism on natural habitats through targeted distribution, video clips, and social media. Towards this the Forest Department and the DWC have developed guidelines and started carrying out awareness programmes for tour guides, and the visitors to parks etc. B esides these, there are the different clubs and collectives, such as the Wildlife Nature Protection Society (WNPS), the Young Zoologists Association (YZA), the Field Ornithology Group of Sri Lanka (FogSL) all carrying out meetings and programmes targeting different interest groups as their names suggest, as well as catering the programmes to different age groups. In addition to agency-led programmes and civil society initiatives, school-based models such as the Schoolyard Scientists programme have supported sustained biodiversity engagement within formal education settings. The initiative has been implemented across multiple provinces. Students and teachers have documented local species within their own school grounds. Regular observation activities have strengthened ecological awareness and empathy toward nature. However, challenges remain. These include limited curriculum time, exam-focused priorities, uneven administrative support, and constraints in long-term continuity. Further progress requires policy integration within the education sector, teacher capacity building, and stronger coordination between schools and national biodiversity monitoring systems. Sri Lanka Marine Protected Area Mapping work done by Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC) in collaboration with Environmental Foundation (Guarantee) Limited (EFL) through the Ocean Country Partnership. Under this initiative a comprehensive map was prepared including all Marine Protected Areas under the FFPO by DWC, Special Management Areas declared by CC&CRMD and Fisheries Management Areas declared by DFAR and all the available coastal marine ecological data. This map will be publicly available through the JNCC and EFL websites. https://jncc.gov.uk/resources/70b74bc6-f67b-483a-8cc1-7c3c999ba674#ocpp-mpa-network-mapping-project.pdf In addition, a variety of local organizations conduct regular awareness programmes aimed at fostering human-wildlife co-existence as well as about the value of environmental stewardship and broader conservation. These reach quite a lot of people. There is also the collective of private sectors, the Biodiversity Sri Lanka (BSL) - a private sector-driven platform to promote corporate engagement in biodiversity conservation, which encourages the private sector to engage in projects related to biodiversity. There are several environmental journalists who also cover topics of biodiversity, although the Sri Lanka Environmental Journalists Forum, once very active is not so currently.  However, there are several new journalist collectives such as the South Asia Women's Media network and the Center for Investigative Reporting (CIR) carrying out programmes of training, webinars titled "Green Dialogue" , etc. There are some very good articles and TV programmes that also cover the topic of biodi ve rsity, often focusing on particularly aspects. The NBSAP set out a plan to develop 10 databases, ranging from the National Biodiversity Database to specific databases of Taxonomic Experts,  Traditional Knowledge; Monitoring Invasive Alien Species (IAS); Genetic Resources; Ecosystem Red List; Trade and Trafficking in Flora and Fauna, Nutritional Quality of Food; and a Web Portal for Ecosystems and Ecosystem Services. Most of these databases were begun, however only some are functioning, either due to funding constraints or changes in personnel. Many of the databases set up, took place through extensive consultative processes, however some of them are not being updated: e.g. the IAS database with a target of being updated every 4 years was developed, but not active. Some of these have seen components fall into place, as with the Green Taxonomy Experts database. With others, policies and action plans have been put in place, but development of the database is to commence. In other cases, although there may not be databases set up by government institutions, yet either through independent projects or environmental NGOs/think tanks, some have been set up. E.g. There is a comprehensive Sri Lankan Food Composition Database (FCDB) set up in 2025, based on the Department of Nutrition, Medical Research Institute, Ministry of Health’s  Publication of the Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (2021); there is also a database developed by Global Sustainability Solutions, on Ecosystems and Ecosystems Services, and handed over to the Ministry, and under consideration on how it can be adopted. There have also been studies on the effectiveness of awareness creation projects. E.g. Studies in the Jaffna Peninsula (2025) showed high awareness (76%) of biodiversity benefits like pollination and pest control, even though populations continued to decline due to habitat fragmentation. Source: "Perceptions, awareness, and conservation challenges of urban wildlife in Jaffna Peninsula, Sri Lanka", published in January 2025. A 2023 study explored the impact of Environmental Sensitivity Training (EST) on the behavior of wildlife tour guides, who act as frontline ambassadors for conservation. This found that the guides with higher ecological knowledge exhibited significantly more responsible wildlife viewing behaviors; and that training programs that incorporated immersive nature experiences and personal development activities had a notably stronger impact on "Environmental Wellness" (WE) and pro-wildlife behaviors (WB) compared to classroom-only sessions. ( https://www.seu.ac.lk/jom/publication/v18n2/JM18_2_04.pdf ).

There are some databases that lie with various agencies, but there is no infrastructure or initiative to bring these together. The cost and lack of skilled database personnel within the MoE could be one reason.

Main Actions Summary: Constitutional Foundations for Biodiversity Protection The Directive Principles of State Policy under the Chapter XI of the 1978 Constitution of Sri Lanka, while non-justiciable on their own, provide essential interpretive guidance to courts and policymakers. Environmental relevance arises particularly from Article 27(14) and Article 28(f). Article 27(14) of the Constitution: stipulates that the State shall protect, preserve and improve the environment for the benefit of the community. Article 28(f): enshrines that it is the fundamental duty of every person in Sri Lanka to protect nature and conserve its riches. Though not expressly defined, the term “riches” should be understood broadly to include: Biological diversity comprising ecosystems, species and genetic resources Cultural, spiritual, and aesthetic values of nature and Natural capital is essential for economic and social well-being. These provisions reflect that the sustainable use and conservation of ecosystems implicit constitutional goals and recognize that nature has value beyond immediate human exploitation. Thereby, they reinforce ethical responsibility toward natural living systems. Sri Lankan courts have relied on Article 12 - which enshrines the fundamental right to equality - to bridge the gap between such non-justiciable directive principles and enforceable rights, thereby strengthening constitutional protection for environmental and biodiversity concerns. Key Legislations for General Protection of Nature National Environmental Act No. 47 of 1980 (as amended) Provides the primary legal framework for environmental protection, pollution control, and environmental impact assessment to ensure sustainable development. Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance No. 2 of 1937 (as amended) Protects wildlife and plant species in Sri Lanka by regulating hunting, trade, and habitat conservation through protected areas and species protection. Coast Conservation and Coastal Resource Management Act No. 57 of 1981 (as amended) Regulates development and activities in the coastal zone to protect coastal ecosystems and promote sustainable coastal resource management. Fisheries and Aquatic Resources Act No. 2 of 1996 (as amended) Governs the conservation, management, and sustainable use of fisheries and aquatic resources in Sri Lanka’s waters. Forest Ordinance No. 16 of 1907 (as amended) Provides for the protection, conservation, and management of forests and forest resources. National Heritage Wilderness Areas Act No. 3 0f 1988 (as amended) Ensures protection, preservation, and management of unique ecosystems, genetic resources, and threatened species of outstanding universal value. Marine Environment Protection Act No. 59 of 2008: Focuses on preventing marine pollution. Sri Lanka Land Development Corporation (SLLDC) Act, No. 15 of 1968 (as amended) governing land reclamation, development, and flood mitigation in Sri Lanka.  It manages water retention areas, lowlands, marshy lands, and swamp lands. A critical amendment in 2006 (Act No. 35) empowered the corporation to take legal action against the pollution of canals and unauthorized activities. Mines and Minerals Act, No. 33 of 1992 - legislation that established the Geological Survey and Mines Bureau (GSMB). It centralizes the ownership of minerals in Sri Lanka and regulates all activities related to the exploration, mining, and trade of these resources. Sri Lanka Customs Ordinance (No. 17 of 1869) is the primary legal framework for regulating imports and exports, collecting revenue, and enforcing border laws in Sri Lanka. The Ordinance is a critical tool for environmental protection, managed primarily through the Biodiversity, Cultural and National Heritage Protection (BCNP) Division . Police Ordinance No. 16 of 1865 and amendments provides the foundational legal authority for the Sri Lanka Police to enforce environmental protection and support specialized conservation. National Policy on Invasive Alien Species (IAS) in Sri Lanka was approved by the Cabinet of Ministers on March 30, 2016. It serves as a comprehensive framework to protect Sri Lanka’s natural and agro-ecosystems from the threats posed by non-native species National Policy on Biodiversity of Sri Lanka (2024 Draft/Proposed): The Biodiversity Division of the Ministry of Environment is currently finalizing an overarching policy to treat biodiversity as critical national capital, aimed at aligning with the 30x30 target. National Policy on Environmentally Sensitive Areas (ESAs): A recent focus focusing on protecting critical habitats outside the formal protected area network. These instruments collectively provide a general legal shield for nature, and for the conservation of living entities in Sri Lanka Judicial Review for the Development of Environmental Jurisprudence in Sri Lanka Public Trust Doctrine Sri Lankan courts have consistently recognised the Public Trust Doctrine, holding that the State does not own natural resources in an absolute proprietary sense but holds them in trust for the people, including future generations. This doctrine has been articulated most clearly in landmark Supreme Court decisions such as Bulankulama v. Secretary, Ministry of Industrial Development (Eppawala case) , Watte Gedera Wijebanda v. Conservator General of Forests And Others, Ravindra Gunawardena Kariyawasam v. Central Environmental Authority and Others(Chunnakam Powerplant case), Centre for Environmental Justice v. Anura Satharasinghe et. al (Wilpattu forest case) and Sarath Fernando, Conservator General of Forests v. P.B.S. Dissanayake and Others. In these rulings, the Court affirmed that: Natural resources such as land, water, minerals, forests, and ecological systems are part of the common heritage of mankind. The State acts as a trustee or guardian, not an unfettered owner. This judicial approach is consistent with the normative foundations of the forthcoming National Biodiversity Policy which reinforces that biodiversity conservation is not merely a discretionary policy choice but a constitutional and fiduciary obligation of the State. Intergenerational Equity Sri Lankan environmental jurisprudence views intergenerational equity as an integral part of sustainable development and biodiversity protection, binding the State and public authorities to responsibly manage natural resources so that environmental quality is preserved not just for the present population, but for those yet to come. Biodiversity loss is irreversible in human timescales; therefore, policy and legal decisions must account for: Rights of unborn generations, Long-term ecological resilience, Ethical obligations beyond short-term economic gains. A National Biodiversity Policy must embed this principle not as rhetoric but as a decision-making criterion. Paradigm Shift from Anthropocentricism to Ecocentrism in Biodiversity Conservation Environmental degradation and biodiversity loss are symptoms of: Anthropocentric worldviews, Unsustainable consumption patterns and A failure to recognize ecological limits. Anthropogenic activities pose the greatest threat to ecosystems and natural entities. Biodiversity governance must therefore integrate legal enforcement with ethical reorientation. Strengthening the legal framework pertaining to biodiversity conservation requires embracing intergenerational equity, empowering citizen guardianship, and fostering a profound shift in humanity’s relationship with the natural world. In light of the anthropocentric nature of Sri Lankan laws, escalating environmental degradation, and scientific warnings, the policy argues for strengthening legal protection for living entities by recognizing the Rights of Nature. It promotes a shift in values from viewing nature as a mere resource to acknowledging its i ntrinsic value and legal standing. Accordingly, the policy reflects an ecocentric approach to environmental governance and it assigns the State a central role in facilitating and overseeing the adoption of the Rights of Nature framework, acknowledging that the protection of the Rights of Nature imposes inherent and immutable obligations and responsibilities upon human society. Access to justice and information related to biodiversity by indigenous peoples and local communities, including gender and intersectional concerns Sri Lanka has made some efforts towards the full, equitable, inclusive, effective and gender-responsive representation and participation in decision-making, and access to justice and information related to biodiversity by indigenous peoples and local communities, yet with limited progress through engaging women and indigenous people in various points,  preserving traditional knowledge, attempts at disaggregated data, increasing women’s inputs and expertise in gender-biodiversity, inclusive biodiversity governance, inclusive capacity development, participation of women and other marginalized groups, integrated reporting mechanisms. As part of the preparation of Sri Lanka’s 7 th National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity, a dedicated consultation was conducted with representatives of all eight identified indigenous Veddah clans, namely Dambana, Pollebedda, Nilgala, Rathugala,Henanigala, Muthur, Dalukana and Wahare, with participation of relevant Officials from the Ministry of Environment. This engagement is considered a positive development, as it reflects the Ministry’s expressed commitment to listening directly to the concerns, experiences and priorities of indigenous peoples and to strengthening dialogue beyond one off consultations. The process provided valuable insights into both progress made and persisting challenges related to the implementation of KMGBF Targets, particularly with regard to participation, rights recognition and access to traditional lands. The following are the key initiatives that have taken place during the reporting period: 1. National observance and cultural preservation of Indigenous Peoples’ Day Sri Lanka has strengthened its formal recognition of indigenous cultural heritage through state level observances of the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples. Since 2025, the Government has held national celebrations at the Indigenous Museum in Dambana, Uva Province, under the patronage of the President and in coordination with the Ministry of Cultural Affairs and other public authorities. These events highlight the historical and cultural identity of the indigenous Veddah community, incorporating traditional rituals, symbolic acts such as planting sandalwood saplings, and exhibitions of indigenous crafts, including indigenous herbal products developed through traditional knowledge. The celebration serves both as a cultural preservation mechanism and as a platform for raising national awareness of indigenous contributions to the country’s cultural diversity. Government participation at the highest-level signals growing institutional recognition of indigenous heritage and supports efforts to integrate indigenous perspectives into broader cultural policies. Yet, the recognition of the other clans tends to be limited even in this event. 2. Progress on legal recognition and protection of indigenous rights In pursuit of enhanced legal protections for indigenous peoples, Sri Lankan authorities have initiated legislative reforms aimed at recognizing and safeguarding the rights of the indigenous Veddah community. In 2023 & 2024, the Sri Lankan Cabinet approved a proposal to introduce new national legislation specifically addressing the rights of indigenous peoples. This decision followed extensive cross-sector consultations and refinement of a concept paper involving relevant Ministries (including Land, Environment, Forest Conservation, Justice and Cultural Affairs) and legal drafting authorities. The Legal Draftsman has been instructed to prepare the draft bill, which is intended to clarify and protect fundamental rights, including tenure and cultural rights. Separately, the Ministry of Environment organized stakeholder engagements with indigenous representatives to review progress on the indigenous rights bill and identify legal and technical barriers to its advancement. Officials stressed the necessity of regulatory frameworks that uphold indigenous rights and freedoms in accordance with constitutional guarantees and international norms. While the draft bill and institutional discussions represent meaningful steps towards fulfilling the commitments under KMGBF Target 22, the legislative process remains ongoing, and final adoption of comprehensive indigenous rights legislation has not yet been completed. Advocacy from indigenous leaders and support from civil society organizations remain critical to ensure that the final law effectively addresses land rights, cultural preservation, and non-discrimination. 3.    Recognition of indigenous territories Although OECMs are not a legally recognised category of protected areas in Sri Lanka it is making significant attempts to make progress under this theme.  Give a list of the ongoing government projects on giving territorial rights to Veddah communities. Mainstreaming Gender and Inclusion of other marginalized communities. Sri Lanka has made efforts at project and community levels in integrating women into biodiversity conservation, sustainable land management, ecosystem restoration, and agro-ecosystem initiatives. Women benefit primarily through livelihood diversification, community-based conservation, and capacity-building programmes implemented by government agencies, private sector actors, and civil society organizations (e.g., MoE Biodiversity Division projects, LDN initiatives, Dilmah Conservation, Biodiversity Sri Lanka, UNDP SGP). However, women’s leadership remains largely operational rather than policy driven. Women’s organizations and Indigenous and Local Communities (IPLCs) have limited direct engagement in formal decision-making related to land tenure, land governance, water resources, and national biodiversity policy reform. Progress Summary: Women and traditional knowledge The stakeholder consultation data indicates that Sri Lanka has made progress at the project and community levels, particularly in biodiversity conservation, sustainable land management, forest and mangrove restoration, and agro-ecosystem initiatives. However, women’s leadership and influence remain largely operational rather than policy-driven, with limited direct engagement of women’s organizations in formal decision-making on land tenure, land governance, and national biodiversity policy reform. Women mostly benefit by livelihood diversification (value-added forest products, traditional foods, agro-based income), Conservation efforts (nursery management, conservation-oriented agricultural and tourism landscapes, community-based conservation) and participating in awareness, training, and capacity-building programmes by public and private actors. e.g.: MOE Biodiversity Division projects / Natural Resource Management and LDN initiatives / Mannankulam (Pvt) Ltd / Dilmah Conservation/ Biodiversity Sri Lanka. Government agencies (MOE, Forest Department, Department of Wildlife Conservation) and research institutions emphasize awareness creation and local consultation, which supports inclusive participation but does not yet fully translate into shared decision-making authority. NBSAP (2016–2022) of Sri Lanka, included strategic targeted actions to promote traditional sustainable uses of biodiversity and recognize traditional knowledge, innovations and practices of indigenous and local communities relevant for conservation and sustainable use. The Sri Lankan chapter of GYBN  ()Official Youth Constituency under the UNCBD) conducted a youth NBSAP analysis and consultation process - with youth from across Sri Lanka ( 30 + ) including indigenous communities in Dambana and   Henanigala. Sri Lanka has a National Policy on Traditional Knowledge and Practices aimed at; conserving and documenting traditional knowledge and practices sustainably, recognizing it as a common resource generated across generations, ensuring documentation and equitable benefit sharing, enhancing community participation in conservation of traditional knowledge by MoE. Sri Lanka adopted the National Policy on Indigenous Medicine (2024-2034), while not exclusively biodiversity policy, it directly supports traditional knowledge preservation especially knowledge held by women community practitioners in indigenous medicine. The policies include language on indigenous knowledge in full alignment with KMGBF. But the existing partial, grassroots level examples are not documented in official reports except for a few.  The following are some examples: Hela Bojun (Traditional Sri Lankan food outlets) programme promotes traditional food systems, often led by women, linking indigenous food knowledge with nutrition and livelihoods. Groups of women farmers supported by UNFPA, are conserving traditional and endemic seed varieties, building seed banks, sharing indigenous agricultural knowledge, and enhancing climate resilience and transmitting traditional farming practices. UNDP’s small grants projects in Sri Lanka are designed to generate knowledge products on indigenous culture, traditions, and indigenous knowledge, including capacity building for indigenous women to produce traditional forest-derived products. IPLC identity and connection with nature The IPLC community in Sri Lanka, maintains a deep spiritual bond with nature, seeking protection from deities (Gana Deviyo, Valli Deviyo, and Kanda Bandara) before entering the forest for hunting or gathering. The restriction on traditional use is significant; there is a clear conflict with wildlife regulations. Also, the human wildlife conflict in IPLC ccommunities living near the Senanayake Samudraya and other areas report ongoing Human-Elephant conflicts. Encroachment & extraction including illegal excavations is occurring in some areas with the growing interest of private businesses which are active in the region. There is a visible threat to cultural identity. While some value their identity, others are reluctant to identify as "Adivasi" (indigenous) when moving to cities. Traditional language is also noted as being in a state of flux or decline. Some youths are pursuing higher education and due to insufficient local resources, many travel to cities like Anuradhapura and Dambulla to find work. Wariga Sabawa (traditional tribal council), indicating that traditional decision-making structures are still functioning and used for discussing natural resource governance and community welfare. Intersection of Biodiversity and the climate with issue of SGBV: Data products explicitly linking GBV & biodiversity in Sri Lanka remain limited, and Sri Lanka’s existing gender climate assessments, disaster GBV handbooks, and national action plans provide a foundation of data and narrative logic that link environmental risk contexts to gender violence vulnerabilities. Multi‑Sectoral National Action Plan on SGBV (2024–2028) of Sri Lanka addresses Sexual and Gender‑Based Violence through coordinated action across sectors (education, health, disaster management, justice, social protection, etc.). This indicates national priorities on SGBV, including structural inequalities that can intersect with disaster and environmental stresses. The plan included a section on indigenous medicine and aims to link traditional health practitioners and practices with SGBV prevention and response, especially in communities where indigenous medicine is widely used with key activities. A practical guidance handbook, created by Sri Lanka’s Disaster Management Centre with UNFPA bridges gender‑based violence with disaster response planning and showing how gender and environment intersect. Gender‑Responsive Climate Security Assessment (2025) is a nationally focused assessment produced by UN Women, UNDP and partners that explores how gender roles and inequalities intersect with climate change impacts and security in Sri Lanka. The policy brief by UNFPA Sri Lanka highlight how climate risks exacerbate gender vulnerabilities, including increased risks of GBV as climate stress grows. Sri Lanka shows foundational progress in gender equality legislation (CEDAW, Constitution and an amendment to Land Development Act) and increasing participation of women in natural resource programmes. However, the specific goal of effectively eliminating and responding to gender‑based discrimination and violence in the context of control, ownership, and access to sustainable use and conservation of biodiversity is still limited in implementation. Overall, protection mechanisms for women environmental defenders and operational measures for park rangers remain underdeveloped. Women’s Inclusion in planning processes: The MoE has appointed three expert committee groups for effective management of critical ecosystems and species with the representation of women experts in biodiversity. There are women effectively integrated into decision-making structures, and their roles show women holding diverse portfolios, including technical decision making, financial decision making, and memberships in high-level committees and district land use planning committees. In the biodiversity workforce at regional level, women are actively seeking and receiving training in professional development and capacity-building programs. In the nonprofit/CSOs/NGOs and individual activist categories in regional level within this specific sample, men are distributed more broadly across the biodiversity sector. While the women currently in the system are contributing to decision-making and implementation, the participation is not yet "full" or "equitable" across the entire sector. Women are involved in Land Use Planning and Resource Management (e.g., Mangrove conservation), which is a key component of recognizing equal rights to natural resources. Women make substantial and multi-level contributions to biodiversity and environmental research and assessments. Their contributions can be grouped into few key areas including biodiversity assessments (flora & fauna), assessment of ecosystem restoration and monitoring, climate change modelling and species distribution (GIS-based), genetic diversity, ex-situ and in-situ conservation, human–wildlife conflict research and studies on home garden agro-biodiversity. Also, the contribution of women is reflected in preparation of national red lists, peer-reviewed publications, book chapters, and research supervision. Gender equality and women’s participation in planning and governance: The 07th NR to CBD of Sri Lanka, utilized an expertise on gender and data collection were done through a desk review of existing literature, in-person consultations with public sector officials, academia, CSO/ NGO / environmental actors, private sector, indigenous people and local communities at national and regional level. The data collected were assessed through a qualitative analysis against the GAP of KMGBF, and as a cross-cutting theme in previous NBASP. Sri Lanka’s biodiversity-related delegations (CBD COPs, SBSTTA, SBI) include women officers from the Ministry of Environment and related institutions were received capacity development on gender equality and governance programmes by UN supported initiatives (e.g. UNDP, UN Women). These programmes strengthen leadership capacity broadly, however, a dedicated national programme specifically targeting leadership, negotiation, and facilitation skills for women biodiversity delegates has not yet been formally established or reported. Sri Lanka has taken several steps to strengthen gender equality and women’s participation broadly, which are relevant to fulfilling the mentioned activities. The first National Action Plan on Women, Peace & Security (2023–2027) was adopted and developed through consultations with women leaders, civil society, and government stakeholders and this plan aimed at boosting women’s input in peacebuilding and governance processes. The NAP on WPS focuses on gender equality, women’s empowerment, peacebuilding, conflict prevention, and recovery. But it emphasizes gender-responsive conflict of recovery and resilience, including considerations related to climate insecurity and community roles. The Ministry of Environment and related agencies are the national focal points for biodiversity (CBD), but there is no clearly reported national “gender and biodiversity” coordination body established as a formal government mechanism (e.g., a standing inter-ministerial working group) in official biodiversity documents that are publicly accessible. Workshops and collaborative engagements have brought women’s organizations and environmental actors together at project or sector level, but these appear project-specific rather than sustained national coordination mechanisms across sectors, As example a policy dialogue on “Sri Lankan Women and Girls in Climate Action” was convened with the Ministry of Environment, UNFPA, UNDP and SLYCAN Trust is an important step toward linking gender and environmental action. However, there is not widely visible formal, permanent coordination body (government-led) dedicated to gender-biodiversity programming as fully operational and reporting progress, and the current arrangements are more project-based and emerging.
Key Challenges Summary: Limited inclusivity and collaboration with all identified indigenous clans: Despite the initiation of national-level observance of Indigenous Peoples’ Day, effective and inclusive engagement with all identified indigenous clans remains limited. Public recognition and related activities have largely centred on the Vedda community of Dambana, while other recognised clans Pollebedda, Nilgala, Rathugala, Henanigala, Muthur and Wahare have received comparatively less visibility and engagement. In addition, there are at least 22 other locations where indigenous presence is believed to exist but has not yet been formally identified. Progress in identifying and engaging these communities has been constrained by limited financial, technical, and institutional resources, resulting in gaps in representation, consultation, and participation. This uneven engagement challenges the equitable and inclusive implementation of Target 22 across the country. Policy implementation conflicts affecting indigenous livelihoods The implementation of sectoral environmental and conservation policies has, in some instances, adversely affected indigenous livelihoods. A recent example is the declaration of the Nilgala Forest Reserve, which, while contributing to biodiversity conservation objectives, has significantly restricted access of indigenous communities to forest areas traditionally used for their subsistence and cultural practices. Such restrictions have disrupted primary livelihood activities and customary use of forest resources. Similar challenges have been reported in other parts of the country, where indigenous individuals have faced arrests or legal action by enforcement agencies, including the Department of Wildlife Conservation, for entering legally protected areas. These situations highlight ongoing tensions between conservation frameworks and the recognition of indigenous customary rights and traditional resource use. In practice, despite the gazette notifications and identity card permitting Indigenous communities to access protected areas for the collection of medicinal plants and other forest-based resources, there have been instances where the Department of Wildlife Conservation has taken such individuals into custody within these areas. In these situations, human rights defenders and environmental organizations have intervened, often resulting in favorable outcomes in court. Example for such cases include court case number – 52921 of Bibila magistrate court. Challenges in identification and legal recognition of indigenous peoples The identification and official recognition of indigenous peoples remain a key challenge. Following displacement during the conflict period and subsequent resettlement, some indigenous individuals have been issued National Identity Cards (NICs) identifying them solely as “Sri Lankan Tamil”, resulting in the loss of formal recognition of their indigenous identity. This has created administrative and legal barriers to accessing targeted support, participation mechanisms, and rights-based interventions. The absence of a nationally agreed definition of “indigenous peoples” further compounds this challenge. At present, there is no clearly defined, nationally endorsed definition at the policy or legal level, which limits the ability of institutions, particularly within the Ministry of Environment and related agencies, to design, implement and monitor initiatives specifically addressing indigenous peoples’ rights and needs. Unclear land rights and delayed legal safeguards Although efforts are underway to introduce dedicated legislation to protect indigenous peoples’ rights, land tenure and land rights remain inadequately defined and legally unclear. Indigenous communities have consistently expressed strong concerns regarding the lack of formal recognition of their customary land ownership and use rights. The absence of enacted legislation providing explicit land rights protection continues to expose indigenous communities to displacement, restricted access and legal uncertainty. Delays in finalising and operationalising the proposed legal framework remain a major barrier to fully achieving the objectives of KMGBF Target 22 in Sri Lanka. Limited participation of indigenous peoples in decision-making and expert processes A significant challenge in implementing KMGBF Targets is the absence of systematic involvement of indigenous peoples in expert committees, advisory bodies and subject-specific decision-making processes that directly affect them. At present, indigenous representatives are generally not included as members of technical committees, expert panels or policy formulation groups related to biodiversity conservation, land management, environmental governance or cultural heritage. This lack of representation limits opportunities for indigenous knowledge, perspectives and lived experiences to inform policies and programmes. Consequently, decisions are often made without adequately reflecting indigenous priorities, customary practices or socio-cultural realities. The absence of institutionalised mechanisms for indigenous participation in governance structures remains a key barrier to achieving the full, effective and inclusive participation envisaged under KMGBF Targets.

Progress Summary: International/ National Policy Environment Sri Lanka's National Policy on Gender Equality and Women's Empowerment (published 12 March 2023 by the Ministry of Women, Child Affairs and Social Empowerment and UNFPA) includes a dedicated chapter on "Environment and Disaster Management," with the policy commitment of enabling the voice and full participation of women, girls and gender minorities in the protection and management of the environment. The policy is strongly aligned with the Aichi Targets and is in several areas more progressive than those targets, particularly on governance, equity and participation. Gender-responsive climate finance Sexual and gender-based violence in disasters Gender minorities (not addressed in Aichi). Sri Lanka’s 2016–2022 NBSAP does not explicitly reference gender equality, women’s land rights, or women’s access to natural resources as biodiversity outcomes; gender is treated as a cross-cutting development issue rather than an operational biodiversity objective. However, Sri Lanka’s draft biodiversity policy, currently progressing towards final adoption, explicitly includes stakeholder engagement and community-driven approaches, and references equity, inclusiveness and gender-responsiveness as guiding principles for biodiversity management . An amendment to the Land Development Ordinance of 1935, passed by Parliament in March 2022, removed the previous bias that gave preference to the eldest male heir. Under the amended law, children of any gender are equally entitled to inherit state-granted land. Previously, Schedule III of the Ordinance gave male heirs priority; the amendment introduced gender-neutral language so that children of any gender fall within the same class of successors. This reform applies specifically to state-allocated land under the Land Development Ordinance and does not automatically eliminate all discriminatory practices in private landownership, customary law, or inheritance outside this system. Other legal frameworks — such as personal laws including Kandyan and Muslim law — continue to influence land and property rights beyond the scope of this statute. Sri Lanka has been a Party to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) since 1994 and participates in related reporting and international biodiversity governance processes, which increasingly incorporate gender considerations under the CBD’s gender-responsive decisions. Sri Lanka’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the UNFCCC explicitly incorporate Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) aspects, recognising the differential impacts of climate change and the need for inclusive climate action that benefits women and other groups. In its climate policy and NDC implementation planning, Sri Lanka aligns biodiversity adaptation priorities with climate action sectors and emphasises social inclusion and gender-responsiveness. Sri Lanka is not a party to the Nagoya Protocol, and global implementation guidance on gender integration within Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) instruments is still being developed at the CBD level and has not yet translated into specific gender-mainstreamed ABS rules within Sri Lanka’s national framework. Sri Lanka’s National Policy on Gender Equality and Women’s Empowerment provides a broad, cross-sectoral framework requiring gender mainstreaming across all national policies, programmes and decision-making processes, to ensure that women and gender minorities have equal participation, access and benefits from development initiatives. While this general gender policy can serve as a basis for integrating gender perspectives into sectoral laws or biodiversity-related instruments such as ABS, it is not specific to ABS. There is limited evidence of targeted, high-profile contributions or joint international activities explicitly advancing gender within the biodiversity frameworks of the Rio Conventions — such as official gender-biodiversity tool development, thematic submissions, or coordinated Rio Convention gender events involving Sri Lanka. 2. Research and Assessment Publicly available documents produced by UN agencies and academics reflect a combination of participatory elements — including Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA) tools and gender-sensitive consultations — with case studies and surveys. Some reports highlight gender gaps using secondary data rather than primary participatory assessments. Inclusive Finance for Biodiversity A number of projects target women for training, capacity-building and income generation, supporting their engagement in biodiversity governance and sustainable use. However, direct measures to improve access to formal financial services and credit remain limited. While formal financial services (bank loans and microcredit) are rarely referenced explicitly, several programmes include alternative income-generation support, including through SMEs, handicrafts, traditional products, and the processing of biodiversity-based resources. The evidence points to broader financial inclusion tools and SME support that women utilise in biodiversity-related sectors, but no dedicated mechanism exists yet for genetic resource benefit‑sharing or biodiversity credit for women. UNDP Small Grants Programme Projects in Sri Lanka: Women’s groups engaged in biodiversity restoration projects, provided with training and support for income-generating activities. Commercial and cooperative banks like CDB / Commercial Bank CSR: Community engagement projects supporting women including financial literacy sessions, small-scale enterprise support, microloans for women’s groups. McLarens Mangrove CSR Project: Women in coastal communities empowered through mangrove restoration, including training in sustainable harvesting, small business opportunities using mangrove resources. Sri Lanka’s participation in UNDP’s Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN) has included certification of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) including certified entities owned by women entrepreneurs. UNDP is funding a project under GEF 07 — Partnerships and Innovative Financing to Mainstream Biodiversity and Sustainable Land Management in the Wet Climatic Zone of Sri Lanka — which includes a strong commitment to gender mainstreaming in biodiversity and sustainable land management at the grassroots level in the estate sector. Sri Lanka’s participation in the BIOFIN process has helped identify biodiversity financing needs and solutions, including sustainable finance frameworks, payment for ecosystem services, and green certification systems. The Global Trust Fund’s work on sovereign green bonds and sustainable bond frameworks supports longer‑term financing for environmental and social projects. The emerging policy frameworks shows potential include biodiversity‑friendly financial instruments that could benefit women. There are no widely documented financial instruments in Sri Lanka specifically supporting women in biodiversity‑focused STEM. However, women‑focused STEM programmes (NSF/ British Council/ UN Women STEM Programme) do help build skills that can be applied to biodiversity work. 4. Community based implementation Sri Lanka has a rich portfolio of biodiversity and community-based initiatives that can inform gender-related assessments including the initiatives carried out by community-based biodiversity projects (Ex: Rainforest Protectors, Negenahiru Foundation, UNDP Small Grants) corporate & private sector biodiversity initiatives (e.g. Dilmah Conservation, McLarens, John Keels foundation) NGO and environmental groups (WildReach, Forest Healing Sri Lanka, FEOSRI Lanka, Lanka Environment Fund). Sri Lanka has practical experience in integrating gender and marginalised groups into biodiversity projects across government agencies, research institutions, the private sector and civil society (e.g., UNDP GEF Small Grants Programme, Rainforest Alliance – Sri Lanka Tea Estates, Commercial Bank of Ceylon PLC, John Keells Foundation, Dilmah Conservation, INSEE Cement biodiversity initiatives, McLarens Mangrove CSR Project). Across many reports from these actors, a recurring gap is the lack of systematic documentation of gender considerations. While biodiversity conservation and community engagement activities are well described, they typically lack gender-disaggregated data, explicit analysis of women’s roles or benefits, and documentation of what approaches work effectively for women and other marginalised groups. As a result, good practices are reported primarily in environmental terms, with limited reflection on gender-responsive outcomes, lessons learned, or gaps. Analysis of progress across the dimensions of representation, participation, justice and access to information reveals specific strengths in local community engagement and traditional knowledge, alongside gaps in the inclusion of youth and persons with disabilities. Most regional actors work directly and extensively with local communities within community-level geographical scopes. Examples show active community involvement in cascade system rehabilitation, mangrove conservation and fisheries management, indicating that participation is effective at the operational level. While youth and children are rarely involved in formal decision-making processes, implementation efforts are often targeted at them, suggesting that young people are active in implementation but significantly underrepresented in higher-level policy-shaping roles. Access to structured training (in-person or virtual) is relatively high, and information is being disseminated through leaflets, handbooks on Good Agricultural Practices (GAP), and school awareness programmes. Systematic records of participation by persons with disabilities are lacking, though some disability rights leaders are engaged in representation and information activities, indicating a significant area for future focus in ensuring truly inclusive participation . Across the range of initiatives, women are involved in many biodiversity activities, but systematic assessments of their roles and gaps within supply chains or sectors remain limited. Existing case studies and project reports could serve as inputs for gender gap analyses, but the data is fragmented across project-level reporting mechanisms. Sharing of findings through webinars and side events is partially practised — mainly by UNDP and corporate CSR actors — but there is no consolidated national platform for sharing gender-focused biodiversity case studies to support decision-making. 5.Value Added Production & Income Generation Several projects have introduced value-added product creation and income generating activities for women. The Biodiversity Division of the Ministry of Environment is implementing an initiative to train estate workers, including women, to manage nurseries and propagate native plant species in tea and rubber plantations. It also provides training for women on value‑-added products using biodiversity resources such as kithul and cinnamon, enabling women to diversify their income through processing and small‑-scale production. While these interventions support women’s empowerment and entrepreneurial opportunities in biodiversity‑-based supply chains, progress remains largely project‑-based rather than institutionalised at the national policy and implementation level. Further effort is needed to scale, document, monitor and mainstream these interventions across all relevant biodiversity supply chains. The Forest Department has undertaken efforts in the conservation and domestication of Rudumbeniya (a plant used in traditional beedi products), making it available as a raw material. Women in marginalised communities benefit by engaging in its collection and processing for income. Mannankulam Pvt Ltd provides job opportunities for local women tied to biodiversity activities on farm landscapes, offers internships for agricultural students with a focus on regenerative agriculture, and provides training for women in preparing traditional dishes as part of cultural and biodiversity value promotion. Ministry of Crab (a private company), in partnership with UNDP Sri Lanka and GEF SGP, supports community‑-based mangrove restoration and provides training for women in eco‑friendly practices. The Rainforest Alliance Tea Estate Biodiversity Champions initiative delivers training in biodiversity‑-friendly agricultural practices for women estate workers in the tea industry, supporting women’s economic roles in sustainable agriculture and increasing access to training, certification knowledge and market opportunities. Dilmah Conservation includes training women in biodiversity protection as part of its conservation initiatives and supports women’s participation in skill development for eco‑-friendly product enterprises and tourism‑adjacent roles. Women in Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs) are actively involved in both traditional and modern economic activities, making diverse contributions to biodiversity and their local economies. Collecting non-timber forest products (NTFPs) such as seasonal forest produce ( Karamba, Damba, Palu, and Weera) is significant in their income generation methods . Also, women enter reserves to collect yams, demonstrating their direct reliance on and interaction with natural resources. The Chena cultivation (Hena) and paddy farming using rainwater reflect the strong link with biodiversity with their traditional practices towards conservation. Young and modern indigenous women are diversifying into creative industries, making handicrafts, flower baskets, and jewellery while elderly, traditional women play a role in traditional medicine; for instance, when a snake bite occurs, they use treatments sourced from the natural resources available within their communities. A significant portion of women are vulnerable and show economic migration; and widows in particular, face extreme economic hardship. 6. Disaggregated Data and Monitoring Mechanisms The Department of Census and Statistics of Sri Lanka collects sex-disaggregated data across many socio-economic and demographic areas and publishes gender statistics. These data come from national censuses, surveys, and administrative records. DCS also aligns with SDG reporting guidance and is part of the national effort to compile SDG indicators disaggregated by sex where possible. However, current DCS data systems prioritise social and economic variables over environmental ones, and SDG reporting in Sri Lanka remains limited in terms of environment-related indicators at the national statistical level. National environment and climate change policy documents increasingly recognise the importance of gender-sensitive data collection, but this recognition is often general and has not yet been integrated into statistical systems for biodiversity. Sri Lanka’s existing statistical and SDG data systems provide a foundation for disaggregated tracking but currently focus mainly on socioeconomic indicators, the environmental and biodiversity statistics largely lack systematic sex disaggregation. Indicator 5.a.1: (a) Proportion of total agricultural population with ownership or secure rights over agricultural land, by sex; and (b) share of women among owners or rights-bearers of agricultural land, by type of tenure. Indicator 5.a.1:(b) share of women among owners or rights-bearers of agricultural land, by type of tenure. Indicator 8.9.2: Number of jobs in tourism industries as a proportion of total jobs and growth rate of jobs, by sex. Additional sex- and demographic-disaggregated data are reported by a small number of other agencies: Risk and vulnerability indices: Data on climate risk exposure (e.g., drought, floods) by sex, age, income levels and disability status (e.g., from vulnerability mapping conducted in climate‑gender assessments) by UNFPA Access to clean water and energy: Proportion of households with safely managed water and clean fuels, disaggregated by sex of household head and rural/urban location. World Bank Gender Data Portal. Existing indicators remain fragmented, largely socio-economic in scope, and rarely operationalised for biodiversity. Gaps are most pronounced in coverage, integration, intersectional disaggregation and systematic implementation. Major gaps persist in Sri Lanka’s progress, including the absence of explicit national funding lines or dedicated financial instruments to support women, Indigenous peoples and local communities within biodiversity policy frameworks; limited use of gender-disaggregated monitoring and reporting in biodiversity finance and planning; and the lack of fully integrated, formal capacity-building programmes on gender-responsive biodiversity. The promising initiatives noted above, however, provide an opportunity to begin establishing such mechanisms. Intersectional disaggregation by age, disability, ethnicity and geographic vulnerability is inconsistently applied. Biodiversity reporting does not currently include gender-responsive outcome indicators, gender audits, or periodic institutional performance reviews under Target 23. A harmonised gender-biodiversity monitoring framework aligned with SDG 5 and SDG 15 remains undeveloped.
Key Challenges Summary: Despite a supportive overarching gender policy framework, the biodiversity policy architecture lacks a dedicated, operational Gender Action Plan specifically linked to the NBSAP. There is no formal gender coordination mechanism within environmental institutions, nor are there designated gender focal points with the technical authority and resources required. Gender commitments have not yet been translated into measurable biodiversity sector targets, performance indicators, or gender-responsive budgeting lines. Additionally, while land inheritance reforms have progressed, broader structural issues such as personal laws, customary tenure systems, and women’s effective control (as opposed to nominal ownership) of land remain insufficiently examined within biodiversity governance frameworks. Clear institutional accountability for implementing Target 23 across biodiversity agencies is currently absent. Existing assessments lack a comprehensive national gender-biodiversity baseline study that systematically analyses women’s roles, access to and control over resources, and decision-making power across ecosystems (forestry, fisheries, agriculture, wetlands, and coastal zones). Standardised gender analysis tools are underused in biodiversity research methodologies, and there is insufficient primary data collection on intra-household benefit-sharing from biodiversity-based income. Intersectional dimensions — particularly disability, age, indigenous identity, estate-sector vulnerability, and economic displacement — are not consistently integrated into environmental assessments. Additionally, there is no centralised repository for gender-responsive biodiversity research to inform national policy. While women’s participation in community-level biodiversity initiatives is visible, there is limited analysis of the quality of that participation — particularly regarding women’s influence in decision-making bodies, leadership roles and conflict resolution mechanisms. Youth and persons with disabilities are referenced but lack structured inclusion pathways in biodiversity governance. Safeguarding measures to address gender-based violence risks in conservation areas are not explicitly integrated into biodiversity programming. Furthermore, there is no national mechanism to document, evaluate and scale gender-responsive community conservation models, resulting in fragmented learning and limited replication. Current interventions focus on training and livelihood diversification but do not systematically assess women’s control over income, ownership of productive assets, access to markets, or bargaining power within biodiversity value chains. There is no national strategy to institutionalise women-led biodiversity enterprises or integrate them into certified green supply chains at scale. Vulnerable sub-groups — including widows, households affected by migration, women with disabilities and indigenous women — lack targeted economic protection measures within biodiversity programming. Additionally, unpaid care burdens and poverty, which directly affect women’s capacity to engage in biodiversity enterprises, are not addressed in programme design. In summary, major gaps persist in Sri Lanka’s progress, including the absence of explicit national funding lines or dedicated financial instruments to support women, Indigenous peoples and local communities within biodiversity policy frameworks; limited use of gender-disaggregated monitoring and reporting in biodiversity finance and planning; and the lack of fully integrated, formal capacity-building programmes on gender-responsive biodiversity. Intersectional disaggregation by age, disability, ethnicity and geographic vulnerability is inconsistently applied. Biodiversity reporting does not currently include gender-responsive outcome indicators, gender audits, or periodic institutional performance reviews under Target 23. For further implementation: The promising initiatives noted above, despite the gaps,  provide an opportunity to begin establishing such mechanisms in the new NBSAP under review, that will enable all women and girls have the opportunity and capacity to contribute to the objectives of the Convention, that considers their rights and access as well as the context to participate and lead in carrying out the actions.  A harmonised gender-biodiversity monitoring framework aligned with SDG 5 and SDG 15 is envisaged in the new plan as well.
